items.title: Loyalty/Rewards and Other Monetary Scams: The Points Guy (Net Interest)
items.text:
**Here's an interesting (but dated) one... from the amazing Substack "Net Interest."**

I had occasion today to look through point and reward economics, and next to central banking or sex trafficking or whatever it must be one of the most despicable industries out there. It's well-known that loyalty cards/rewards schemes are fiat money-printing scams that, at best, saddles the user with a below-mininum wage job (https://stacker.news/items/869415).

...but it's good for the companies running these schemes. (Yea, no shit: the money printing/issuing was always great, and under shitty monetary regime there's an incentive for everyone to become a bank or a bank-like entity #[743123](https://stacker.news/items/743123), https://stacker.news/items/1329539)

It's a typical example where businesses do things **against the interest of their customer** (thus, it's dishonest) *while looking* like they're providing you with extra benefits. Somebody should call Lizzy (Warren!). (Also, it's one area where the European Union, in its infinite overlording wisdom, made a limiting regulation that was *actually good* for us Europooreans! By capping interchange fees, they basically outlawed rewards programs and saved/spared 500 million Europeans the time/necessary effort to play these silly money games.)

***

In the age of card networks and (FX) spreads (https://stacker.news/items/1586158) and costs to merchants, the COST and BENEFITS of these (Ponzi?) schemes become entirely intransparent where everyone, like in democracy, think they might get one over on someone else.

At best, it's a selection-biased gamble where **sophisticated consumers take advantage by optimizing the terms/conditions/value of the whole scheme vs naive consumers** who mistakenly believe they can/will win, while the house (as every properly set-up gamble) wins. The naive consumers will inevitably make some sort of error in their financial behavior (overdrafts, not enough spending, not maximizing rewards, too small fish such that annual fee eats up all other benefits).

The most well-known examples here are

* **bank deposits**: people hold too much cash at low-yielding bank accounts vs what they could/optimally should keep in higher-yielding savings accounts. The difference, while maaaybe sometimes convenient for the customer, end up in aggregate securing a massive windfall (=cheap financing) for the banks
* **life insurance products**: life insurance is usually priced very affordably and attractively for the buyer, which the insurance company isn't doing out of ignorance or stupidity but because they know from experience that some portion of the buyers (accidents, life circumstances changing, or just neglect) will let their policies lapse after having paid for a few years, meaning free money for the company, or worse, sell it back to the company at a great discount (=again, free money)

Here's the conclusion from a Fed paper on the subject from a few years ago:

> regardless of income, sophisticated individuals profit from reward credit cards at the expense of naïve consumers. To probe the underlying mechanisms, we exploit bank-initiated account limit increases at the card level and show that reward cards induce more spending, leaving naïve consumers with higher unpaid balances \[...]
> Naïve consumers might underestimate these payments and incur costs from usage. Sophisticated consumers, in contrast, might rake in the benefits while avoiding the payments and thus profit from usage

Here's the graph they use to display the idea (sorted by FICO scores, but the same point stands)

![](https://m.stacker.news/162147)

*tl;dr*, the area between the curves is larger on the negative side than the positive side, thus a) redistributing from naive to sophisticated, but more importantly b) makes the entire scam profitable to the company to run: What it has to pay the sophisticated winners is less than what they manage to extract from the idiot losers.

## The entire edifice is a combination of beggar-thy-neighbor and race to the bottom, with misperception and money illusion becoming key features.

From our pal Matt Levine in a recent Money Stuff piece

> banks make a lot of their money from depositor inattention: When interest rates go up, bank customers mostly don’t move their money, because it would be a pain, so banks can pay below-market interest rates on their deposits.
> You could have similar worries about life insurance, or annuities, or mortgages: Lots of financial products are built (and priced) based on assumptions about customer inattention.

The strategy is that you intentionally misprice (underprice) your service, banking on the fact that, in aggregate, enough people who opt in for this juicy, nice-looking offers will make enough errors that the few sophisticated customers who take perfect, optimized advantage of the mispricing won't cost the company.

***

ANYWAY, **Marc Rubenstein walks through the logic and economics of loyalty programs** and points(!) to some of the intricate cross-subsidized and legal/economic oddities with these programs:

> A key question in the whole points dynamic is how much partners pay for miles. Avios Group deferred revenue at a rate of 0.88 pence per point on the stock it issued in 2023, its highest rate in many years. The consumer value of points varies widely according to how they are used, but The Points Guy puts the value of Avios at around 1.2 pence per point, so the benefit to the consumer is clear. 
> Because the airline can adjust the redemption rate to encourage the use of rewards in ways that reduce their marginal cost, it is able to offer rewards to card issuers at a discount.2 In this way, reward programs can generate profits for both issuers and airlines while generating loyalty to both, a significant positive sum outcome.

## “By minting points, airline companies are able to lock in substantial cash flows.”

> Online points-monitoring sites posting point “valuation” tables on a regular basis because of course the offers change and of course the issuer of this fake, unusable money manipulate it to their advantage.
> The only problem is that competition has been driving up the rate at which card companies pay rewards. Over the last 12 months, American Express has paid out 1.07% of purchase volume in rewards, up from 0.80% ten years ago. Other card issuers have seen similar reward inflation. Capital One paid out 1.29% of purchase volume in 2022, up from 0.80% in 2013. And Discover paid out 1.43%, up from 0.94%. 
> American Express was initially exempt from the EU rules, so my British Airways co-branded card remained unaffected. In 2018, though, the courts brought Amex into line. Fortunately, American Express agreed to eat the cost. My BA Premium Plus card continues to pay 1.5 Avios points for every £1 spent, equivalent to around 1.8% on the basis of The Points Guy’s 1.2 pence per Avios valuation. I guess I do pay £250 per year for the privilege, and Amex likely bought the points at a steep discount (in particular the batch they acquired in 2020 to help the airline out of a liquidity squeeze).

JUST that gives us a few intransparent economic flows:

* First: The Amex bailout of BA during ‘rona, purchasing made-up points at cheap discount… even if Amex nominally loses \~1.3% per dollar of EU transactions, if what they hand over to the customer in rewards (=made-up BA money) was acquired at well below par, there’s still a profit in it for the card company.
* Second, to recoup the yearly card fee of 250 quid, a user needs to transact just below £14,000 a year, basically most of the discretionary card spending for a normal (Europoorean) person… and that’s not giving you pounds back, but made-up BA money you must do some additional trixing (in their webshops, for air fares, for lounge access or extra luggage etc) to benefit from.

## “there are clear subsidies at play. Someone, somewhere is subsidizing my points habit – no longer the merchant, it is now other BA or Amex customers. Indeed, such subsidies are the most controversial aspect to the model.”

I don't quite understand what this percentage is referring to (a larger share of Amex revenues are going back to users than before...?) but it seems to suggest that there is some sort of competitive pressure to close this rent-seeking gap

![](https://m.stacker.news/162156)

items.title: Why isn't bitcoin used for more gray market things?
items.text:
@spiral published The Long Road to Bitcoin Payments https://stacker.news/items/1603307/r/Scoresby last week and got quite a good discussion going here and on [Github](https://github.com/spiralxyz/bitcoin-payments/discussions/1).

Today, they are out with a summary of the community's response.

> **1. Global entrepreneurs, human or agent, earning in bitcoin.**
> **2. Agentic payments.**
> **3. Self-custody as stablecoins get more regulated and freezable.**

The guys on PBJ also did a recap of the discussion on their most recent episode, which is an interesting listen:

https://x.com/PresidioPod/status/2118070779959017814

There were two things that caught my attention in this conversation. First, @moneyball makes the point that it is surprising that the gray-market areas haven't seemed to find much use for bitcoin. 

# Why haven't the porn sites, online gambling dens, and illegal markets shown much interest in bitcoin payments?

While moneyball doesn't mention it, he made me think of Starbackr https://stacker.news/items/135689 https://stacker.news/items/67590 and after a little poking around it looks like they had some trouble with the App Store allowing zaps https://stacker.news/items/219407 but eventually managed a workaround https://stacker.news/items/224893 but then pivoted to AI https://stacker.news/items/250739 and quietly shut down -- at least the main starbackr website is no longer reachable (wayback machine last crawled it in [July 2024](https://web.archive.org/web/20240727123411/https://starbackr.com/) and shows a redirect to getcurrent.io -- last crawled by the wayback machine in Dec 2024 -- although you can still reach the [starbackr docs page](https://docs.starbackr.com/)). These guys seem to have made as good a run as any at delivering a bitcoin powered OnlyFans. What happened?

It seems that the same is true for online gambling (although maybe this story about [Iranian gambling sites](https://www.reuters.com/investigations/illicit-iranian-gambling-network-helped-pull-off-4-billion-sanctions-dodge-2026-07-31/) is a hint that bitcoin is being used in this manner? possibly we are all just too goody-goody to get invited to the illegal tables?).

I don't believe that traceability is the answer. As far as I can tell, porn sites and online gambling are mostly using credit card payments and tradfi banking, which is even worse for privacy. 

Spiral says that a lot of responses pointed out that there isn't any demand for bitcoin. But that seems to be answering the question with the question itself -- why isn't there any demand? 

# Surely someone needs money that no one can stop you from sending or receiving?

items.title: When “Nothing Ever Happens” Become the Pennies-Before-Steamroller Trade
items.text:
I’ve never thought I have much of a trading acumen — not in the stock market, not in timing the Bitcoin market (which I clearly cannot…), not in prediction markets. Prediction markets is the [biggest thing I’ve (mostly) changed my mind](https://stacker.news/items/1556891) on this year, and Predyx has been the outlet for me to play in this degenerate pool of trading nonsense. (Maybe I'll move on to the big leagues one day if I feel confident enough!)

And because most things on prediction markets are nonsense, they’re *ripe* for an age-old trading strategy called **Nothing Ever Happens**; it’s basically to buy No contracts on more or less everything. Matt Levine [summarizing](https://archive.md/B2XkB) the idea:

>  the “Nothing Ever Happens” factor: Bettors on prediction markets seem to be biased in favor of stuff happening (because that’s more fun), so betting “No” on every event seems to have positive returns. \[…] because betting heavy favorites is boring and betting underdogs is exciting, there might be positive returns to taking the other side and betting on the heavy favorites.

If there’s a contract like **Will X happen in 2026?** Den is likely a holder on the No side.

![](https://m.stacker.news/163325)

Yes, fine: I have some directional bets too (like the F1 or the Brazilian election… and look how those turned out).

In Prospect Theory, a branch of behavioral economics, there’s the phenomenon of a “sure thing” — basically that people are willing to unreasonably pay up to shove a risk/payoff from 1% (99%) to 0% (100%). *All insurance markets are predicated on this insight* (and customer inattention/monetary misperception…https://stacker.news/items/1598937, https://stacker.news/items/1598123)

At Predyx, I’ve found myself harvesting this quite a bit. I routinely pump sats into [the Saylor trade](https://beta.predyx.com/market/will-strategy-reach-905000-btc-holdings-from-purchases-completed-in-2026-1776280186) … (https://stacker.news/items/1602523) "Will Duolingo add bitcoin payments?" "Will Cuba be attacked by the US?" Those sorts of ridiculous contracts.  

All three technically carry some risk but are *basically* just interest rate trades at this point, and I’m happy to harvest that (steamroller) return.

Same goes for the “Will Bitcoin Hit $x? this year?” which *do* have some hedging benefits but largely suffer from exactly that same excitement mispricing.

## 2 Other Lessons from Trading

1. Which I learned in the Argentina game against Egypt (?) when they were down like crazy but managed to turn it around. While on a walk I saw Argentina trading at 1% and I YOLOd in the biggest Predyx order I’ve ever made — I keep sizes *very* conservative; the emphasis is on *play* in “play money” — and made a total *killing* on this contract. Consequently, in the F1 trade I bought Verstappen contracts at roughly 0. Didn’t care that I’m throwing away sats as long as there was still a mathematical possibility that this flying Dutchman could turn things around — a feat we’ve seen him accomplish in the recent past. (This was also a nice hedge to my 30,000 sats on Antonelli winning, which is but two points of guaranteed now.)
2. When you’re playing the safety/arbitrage/steamroller trades, getting even a single trade wrong is *extremely expensive*… If I’m capturing tons of different 95-5 trades, and all bets are equal-sized (which they are not, and I can monitor/trade on event news etc), getting *one* trade wrong obliterates the profits of nineteen others. *Ouch*. When I do things like this I better not be wrong… More specifically, I size the positions accordingly. A few months ago I wasn’t particularly convinced that the **Saylor>905k BTC contract would be a No**, so all I did was trade around and place small bets (100s of sats). After monitoring their recent Monday-reported purchases and realizing how far away they were from 905k + mapping out the BTC/USD and STRC scenarios, I grew more convinced that this will not work out for Mr. Saylor and his choirbois (*this* side of 2026 — or ever…?)

This win rate (83%) is *way too low* for largely speaking doing steamroller/Nothing-Ever-Happens trades. (Then again, I *have* taken some directional and spicy bets, e.g., during the World Cup, so maybe that’s why)

**In the Brazil election bet yesterday**, I noticed how uncomfortable I was with such a directional bet — on the bloody finish line. The Polymarket reference rate wobbled a little bit, and Den instantly took some profits. *If you hold a contract at ^0.71, there’s a long way down to 0 if you’re wrong.*

…and, election tampering or as fate would have it, I got to experience exactly that. What’s worse, I had timed my social engagements such that I wasn’t in a position to trade *during the most critical hours*. Stupid.

That was an unforeseen/unexpected error. It’s not just *trading* the contracts on their own merits but *whether* I can, practically speaking, make them work. That’s a good lesson, too.

items.title: Microsoft is a Financial Engineer: Cash Flow Questions (FT, Kim & Armstrong)
items.text:
**Back to stock analysis basics!** [https://stacker.news/items/85150\&#x36](https://stacker.news/items/85150&#x36);**,** https://stacker.news/items/836811

*How's Microsoft doing?!*

![](https://m.stacker.news/164439)

## IT's All Just Financial Engineering?!

*Always has been*, idiot. https://stacker.news/items/1604239, https://stacker.news/items/1598123

> Last week, we wrote about how investors in the hyperscalers — Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle — are suddenly taking the decline in the companies’ free cash flow very seriously. (As, naturally, are the rating agencies — S\&P Global cut the outlook on Meta to negative just the other day, citing “significant uncertainty around capex and free operating cash flow”.)
> Microsoft stands out — it appears that, unlike its peers, it is not spending most or all of its cash profits that operations bring in. Correspondingly, Microsoft is the only one of the bunch with positive stock market returns over the last, bruising month:

![](https://m.stacker.news/164440)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164441)

and we care about this *why?*

> Investors like to look at free cash flow because metrics like operating profit and net income capture investment spending only through a smoothed measure (depreciation) and **do not capture swings in working capital items** (such as inventory, receivables and payables) that can dramatically affect a company’s economic position. Hyperscaler investors are, understandably, focused almost exclusively on the investment just at present.

* **GOOD** free cash flow is "fundamental profitability of the business." Selling stuff, you know, the good ole' fashioned reason to be in commerce. (LOL, say the diluting treasury companies... you can just scam your shareholders! https://stacker.news/items/1292636)
* **BAD** free cash flow is about financing (don't mention it to Saylor): terms, timing, BNPL on a corporate level, basically. 

> For example, a business might be able to pay its suppliers very slowly, while extracting instant payment from customers, which creates a growing stream of cash so long as sales are expanding.

## "This sort of financial engineering is not cheating and the company is admirably transparent about it."

> It is a source of real cash that can pay bills, be invested or simply collect interest. Indeed, there is a whole class of businesses that do nothing but co-ordinate various pools of capital with different financing arrangements. **They are called banks.** But free cash flow from financial engineering is often more volatile, less sustainable and harder to scale than cash that flows from profitable non-finance operations.

lol *sick buuuuurn!*

> Dave Zion of Zion Research Group [thinks](https://www.zionresearchgroup.com/blog/microsoft-s-free-cash-flow-would-be-negative-if-not-for-financial-engineering/) that *all* of Microsoft’s free cash flow comes from financial engineering. He thinks this engineering takes four main forms:

![](https://m.stacker.news/164442)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164443)

> The total of these and a few smaller adjustments is $75.3bn last year — more than 100 per cent of the company’s free cash flow. This does not mean that Microsoft is somehow hoodwinking investors. Powerful companies can extract good financial terms from suppliers, customers and investors and these terms have real value.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164444)

*Financial engineer? YES, I AM!* https://stacker.news/items/1514881?commentId=1514971

TL;DR, if you wanna fake (some portion) of your success, you can just print shares. In Saylor's case, it's to pay for expenses and interest to other shareholders (=Ponzi structure); for Microsoft it's to pay for employee compensation and capex.

items.title: If you're running LND, you may be vulnerable to a Linux kernel exploit
items.text:
Easiest thing to do is just shutdown LND for now if you aren't sure. I just did that myself (it's 7am here...)

This is *not* LND's fault. But golang sockets support the mptcp protocol by default, and unpatched linux kernels can be remotely exploited via mptcp via [CVE-2026-98432](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-98432). So if this command returns anything:

```
ss -Mlnp
```

...you are potentially vulnerable.

The fix is upgrading to a kernel that you know is not exploitable and restarting. Or even easier, just disabling mptcp. Heck, do both:

```
echo 'net.mptcp.enabled=0' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-disable-mptcp.conf && sudo sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/99-disable-mptcp.conf && sudo ss -Mlnp
```

items.title: Latest Strikes #42 - October 12th-18th 2026
items.text:
Welcome to Latest Strikes, your weekly report of the latest Lightning-related news. In today's issue, we cover Lightning Labs' new scaling proposition, an interesting cross-layer routing protocol, and more!

![](https://m.stacker.news/162823)

## Lightning Labs Unveils LayerTree

Lightning Labs [unveiled](https://x.com/lightning/status/2110812651882217677) [LayerTree](https://layertree.tech/), a new scaling protocol with 2 core characteristics:

* many (thousands to tens of thousands) users share one single on-chain UTXO, while retaining unilateral exit rights;
* a user leaving the tree requires only one on-chain transaction, independent of the number of users in the tree.

To simultaneously realize these 2 often contradictory properties, LayerTree leverages an off-chain Merkle-sum tree to keep a record of balances, and a set of yet-to-be-activated opcodes (basically, covenants). The exact set of opcodes depends on the targeted implementation (or maybe the other way around), with the minimal version requiring `OP_CAT` and `OP_TWEAKADD`.

[Paper](https://layertree.tech/paper/main.pdf) | [StackerNews Discussion](https://stacker.news/items/1596351/r/fanis)

## Lexe Connect

Lexe unveiled [Lexe Connect](https://docs.lexe.tech/lexeconnect/), a protocol and [specification](https://github.com/lexe-app/lexe-connect) that lets apps request scoped access to your Lexe node. As a reminder, [Lexe](https://www.lexe.app/) is a self-custodial Lightning wallet featuring an LSP, where the node runs in a remote [TEE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trusted_execution_environment) (Trusted Execution Environment) rather than on your phone[^1].

Such a feature makes a lot of sense in Lexe, since it means you can have one always-online Lightning node and connect your apps to it, rather than having one wallet, often custodial, baked into each app. All this with no channel management, since the LSP takes care of that.

[StackerNews Discussion](https://stacker.news/items/1594737/r/fanis) | [YouTube Demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bh951sWxP3Q)

## Landfall

Speaking of Lexe, Vincenzo Palazzo [unveiled](https://x.com/PalazzoVincenzo/status/2107915680465219605) [Landfall](https://github.com/vincenzopalazzo/landfall), an app (web, desktop and agent CLI) aimed at making it easier for Ocean miners to receive their payouts in Lightning. As Palazzo explains, one of the hiccups is that Ocean requires the miner to sign a message using [BIP322](https://bips.xyz/322), which is not often offered by Lightning wallets. Ocean miners hence [need](https://ocean.xyz/docs/lightning#:~:text=A%20Lightning%20node%20supporting%20BOLT12) to find a Lightning wallet that supports Bolt12 and a way to sign a message with the same seed used by the wallet.

Landfall does precisely that: it generates a new seed, displays it to the user for backup, and uses it to both create a new Lexe wallet (and node)[^2] and sign the requested message. What was previously quite the headache becomes only a few steps, easy to follow for anyone who has already set up a wallet before.

Disclaimer: as Palazzo puts it, "Landfall is a showcase, not a production wallet".

## Cassis

[Cassis](https://cassis.cash/) is an interesting formalization (as a protocol) of the idea that multiple Bitcoin layers can be composed in a single payment, as long as each of them supports HTLCs. While such composition is already routinely used today, it's often (always?) limited to one transition: paying a Lightning wallet from a Cashu mint, doing a swap between Liquid and Lightning, depositing on an Ark with a Lightning payment, etc. There might be multiple hops involved in the Lightning part of the payment itself, but there's only one additional hop before or after this Lightning part. While it's theoretically possible to bridge across even more layers in a single payment **atomically**, it becomes a manual process rather than something that happens behind the scenes when the user hits "Pay"[^3].

Cassis simplifies all that with a routing protocol. Nodes advertise which networks they support through Nostr (e.g. a specific Fedimint instance, Lightning, Liquid, a specific Ark, on-chain Bitcoin, etc.) and can be reached through [iroh](https://www.iroh.computer/) when someone wants to route a payment through them. This is basically onion routing, but instead of routing nodes passing down and peeling an onion, the payer's wallet coordinates the whole payment by pinging each node when it's their turn to forward the payment[^4]. So not onion routing at all. Should we call it Cassis Routing?

I think it's great to have a formalized protocol implementing and coordinating multi-layer hops. Of course, it's still very early, but I'll be very curious to see if it catches on!

[Delving Bitcoin Post](https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/cassis-a-new-simple-scheme-for-generic-multi-layer-multi-hop-htlc-routing/2952) | [StackerNews Discussion](https://stacker.news/items/1591643/r/fanis)

## Zeus Release

Zeus v13.2.3 was [released](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/releases/tag/v13.2.3), fixing bugs and bringing the usual amount of improvements and security hardenings. A few editorial picks:

* the embedded LDK node was bumped to version 0.2.7 of rust-lightning, bringing in LDK's October 1st [security release](https://lateststrikes.com/s/2026-38-39-40-41#ldk-release);
* for receiving, Zeus [now](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4673) checks that the invoice wrapped by the LSP matches the one it initially generated, before showing it to the user;
* LNURL-Auth [now](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4576) checks that the callback host matches the signing domain, preventing a class of man-in-the-middle attack where a malicious party could pose as the website the user wants to connect to, and intercept the valid login to access the victim's account on the website themselves;
* Zeus can [now](https://github.com/ZeusLN/zeus/pull/4658) parse (and thus, pay) [BIP353](https://bips.xyz/353) records that contain more than one payment method, e.g. a silent payment address and a Bolt12 Offer. Neat!
* and many, many more things. Check the release notes for more details.

[StackerNews Discussion](https://stacker.news/items/1594119/r/fanis)

## Quick Strikes

* Alby Hub [v1.24.3](https://github.com/getAlby/hub/releases/tag/v1.24.3) was released, bringing back on-chain <> Lightning swaps, and many improvements and bug fixes. Note that this is not the latest, since [v1.24.4](https://github.com/getAlby/hub/releases/tag/v1.24.4) was released yesterday;
* the ([sunset](https://x.com/nixbitcoinorg/status/2087880779892158679)) nix-bitcoin project was [rebooted](https://x.com/PavolRusnak/status/2110300699070537897) as [bitcoinix](https://github.com/bitcoinix/bitcoinix) by a group of developers, including Trezor co-founder Pavol Rusnak;
* [Lightning in a Jar](https://lightninginajar.xyz/) (LiJ) is a browser on-chain and Lightning wallet, powered by [LDK](https://lightningdevkit.org/) compiled to WebAssembly. The team is also building [LIJOX](https://lightninginajar.xyz/#lijox), an open list of LSPs that any LND operator can join by running an adapter on top of their node. They're [looking for](https://stacker.news/items/1596404/r/fanis) such operators to give it a try, as well as eyes on their LDK patch set.
* [lxdev](https://lx.dev/) (we covered their dark pools prototype [here](https://lateststrikes.com/s/2026-30#quick-strikes)) announced [Zark](https://hackmd.io/@januszgrze/HJlHensozl), a privacy-focused blinded statechain protocol that basically tries to improve on [MercuryLayer](https://mercurylayer.com/)'s design by adding zero-knowledge to further reduce the (already small) level of information leak when transacting on the statechain. It's definitely great to see the privacy-focused approach of statechains make a comeback!

***

That's it for last week! Thank you so much for reading this far, and until next week!

[^1]: Basically [Phoenix](https://phoenix.acinq.co/) in the cloud. Which makes sense for a bird.

[^2]: This leverages a yet-unreleased feature of Lexe that lets users bring their own seed when provisioning a new node.

[^3]: For example, you could initiate an Ark onboarding, take the on-chain address returned by the server, use it as the destination of a Lightning-to-bitcoin atomic swap, and pay the Lightning invoice returned by the swap service from your Cashu wallet.

[^4]: More precisely, the payer's wallet first builds a route, and sends a `prepare` message (through iroh) to each node in that path. Each of them can review the terms (amount, fees, destination, involved networks, etc.) and accept or reject. Once all accept, the payer's wallet locks the route and initiates the payment, sending an HTLC to the first node, and sending them an `execute` message, which contains details about the incoming HTLC. The first routing node proceeds to forward the payment to the next node, using another HTLC, and reports back to the payer. The payer then uses the information from this response to send an `execute` message to the next node, with details about the incoming HTLC from the first routing node, and so on.

items.title: [REVIEW] V for Vendetta by Alan Moore and David Lloyd
items.text:
**Normally, I try to avoid spoilers in my reviews. This one has spoilers.**

![](https://m.stacker.news/164947)

V is cool and all and his vendetta against Big Brother is a great story, but there's one part of this that I just can't get out of my mind. In the middle of the story, Evey is captured and thrown in a prison where she is interrogated, tortured, presented with a false confession, and told to sign. She refuses. She doesn't betray V. And so she is told that she is going to be taken out back and shot.

It's a horrible moment. Till now, V has always swooped in to save the day. And throughout Evey's horrible captivity and torture, we keep expecting V to show up and put a stop to it, with knives, mayhem and murder. But, this time, he doesn't show.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164948)

So it seems like this is the end. Evey chooses to stand for what she believes in, even though it means she will die. But then:

![](https://m.stacker.news/164949)

This is a weird twist. But it quickly turns dark when Evey walks through her prison door...and into V's sitting room:

![](https://m.stacker.news/164950)

We knew V was not the most even-keeled individual, but this is messed up. What the hell is going on?

> "Happiness is a prison, Evey. Happiness is the most insidious prison of all."

V has this moment where he completely flips Evey's worldview:

> "I didn't put you in a prison, Evey. I just showed you the bars...You were born in a prison. You've been in a prison so long, you no longer believe there's a world outside...You can feel freedom closing in upon you. You're afriad because freedom is terrifying."

I really struggled with this scene. Evey's conversion seems so unbelievable to me. Why should she see this new injustice (V's little false-flag operation on her) as anything other than the same sort of brutal, banal, boring violence brought down upon her by someone else? Is it that this time she accepted death, no longer trying to bargain with the system? Or that in this case it came upon her from someone she trusted, a quarter she thought was safe?

At first, I thought this was a sort of ends-justify-the-means argument: V's still the good guy here because putting her in a cell and waterboarding her and telling her she's going to be shot gets her to the point where she can be truly free. And it is sort of that, but not entirely.

There's also the blunt force thought that hardship, extreme hardship is a necessary step to freedom -- even perhaps that you can't have freedom without it. This is terrifying because it makes me worry that I am one of the prisoners who would rather remain a prisoner. Because life in prison is happy enough. Maybe you can't get to the freedom without the hardship.

Evey's conversion is successful because the stakes were so high -- she couldn't come to value her life until it was actually on the line. 

This is pretty directly relevant to Bitcoin -- especially this year: if Bitcoin is our shot at freedom, why do we think it will come easy and without terror? Using Bitcoin means you using something designed to break the law. Holding your own keys means you can lose your own keys. 

It's a nice story...but is it true?

items.title: The Kelly Criterion and the Risk of Ruin
items.text:
A few things came together for this. TRADING disasters and prediction market interests (and having to consult [Kelly on something](https://stacker.news/items/1602534?commentId=1604653)); Sam Bankman-Fried on [*The Economist*](https://www.economist.com/finance-and-economics/2026/10/22/sam-bankman-fried-says-he-has-paid-his-debts)’s podcast; Rob Hamilton’s [Lugano lecture](https://x.com/Rob1Ham/status/2115569802316235133) on the “risk of ruin” topic; *and* revisting/publishing notes from Michael Lewis’ [*Going Infinite*](https://link.amazon/B0fLOxPnC) book (https://stacker.news/items/1604939) that I never ended up using for anything.

*A roadmap:*

1. **Who THA HELL is Kelly** and why should I “criterion” my trades after him?
2. **The Mathematics** of the Kelly Criterion
3. **Applications of Kelly,** and Predyx Bets

***

## #1: Who Is Kelly? Why Should I Care?

John Kelly (mid-1900s), American physicist at Bell Labs. Kelly, influenced by Shannon and the rest of the cool mid-20th C gang, studied how info could be transmitted imprecisely and thought about how to interpret the information received like a gambler operating on noisy tips.

The [1956 paper](https://www.princeton.edu/~wbialek/rome/refs/kelly_56.pdf) is what immortalized him, and which traders and financial economists have invoked ever since (though, as always, history took the cumbersome route via others, such as Edward Thorp and [*Beat the Dealer*](https://link.amazon/B0ddiFneW) from 1962). The optimal strategy, Kelly/Thorp found, was to maximize the **long-run** growth of wealth… **not** every individual bet.  

Clanker summary:

> By the late 20th and early 21st centuries the Kelly criterion (often in fractional form—half-Kelly or less—to reduce volatility and account for estimation error) had become a standard tool in professional gambling, quantitative trading, and portfolio construction. It is frequently associated with investors such as Warren Buffett, Bill Gross, and Jim Simons, though exact usage varies and is sometimes debated.

## #2 The Mathematics of the Kelly Criterion

The Kelly Criterion, then, maximizes *the expected logarithm of wealth* (or: the long-run geometric growth rate of a stock of capital, such as betting pot… you only have so much money/liquidity to play with, and for e.g., a portfolio manager at a hedge fund, only so much allocated to *you* and your trades). This *isn’t* maximizing expected value (arithmetic return), which would tell you to bet everything on every positive-EV opportunity—and would almost surely lead to ruin after a string of losses.

*How?*

The issue with using positive-EV only as your trading strategy is the “[sequence of returns](https://www.schwab.com/learn/story/timing-matters-understanding-sequence-returns-risk)” risk/asymmetry: after -50% return you need +100% *just* to get back. It usually comes up in [retirement/safe-withdrawal conversations](https://investmentmoats.com/budgeting/retirement-planning/explaining-sequence-of-return-risk-and-possible-solutions/), but Morgan Rochard invoked it for Bitcoiners (and their often too-risky personal finances, https://stacker.news/items/1604905) in her recent [appearance on SLP](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K0Y3hI5YBH4) also.  

The Kelly criterion tries to account for that risk by avoiding overbetting when there’s risk of ruin. Most gamblers and traders use half or quarter Kelly as a “margin of safety” (per Warren Buffett), because:

* You don’t *exactly* know the probabilities and payoffs;
* There are TX costs, taxes, and quite often constraints on liquidity (St Petersburg paradox https://stacker.news/items/1585258);
* Unwilling to tolerate extreme volatility/drawdowns;
* Your utility function *isn’t* linear (unless you’re Sam Bankman-Fried, see below https://stacker.news/items/1604939) but logarithmic/diminishing returns.

Half-Kelly, googling tells me, “typically captures about three-quarters of the maximum growth rate while cutting volatility roughly in half and dramatically reducing the probability of large drawdowns.”

It’s similar to the Secretary Problem (https://stacker.news/items/1599572), where you’re trying to balance/optimize between time spent interviewing and the difference in final outcome; only here you’re balancing reaping long-term gains but minimizing volatility/drawdowns.

Simple formula (for a bet that pays net odds (b) to 1, with win probability (p), and loss probability q= 1-pq= (1-p):

![](https://m.stacker.news/164218)
...where f\* is the optimal *fraction* of your investable pot (“bankroll”) to bet…

BASICALLY: bet your *edge* https://stacker.news/items/735212 — meaning **the difference between what you think the value of an asset is** (what the contract *should* trade at) and **what it’s currently trading for** (the rate the contract/betting book offers) — *divided* by the odds.

Basic example is an uneven (60-40) coin flip with even payoffs. This is stupidly +EV but betting all, half, or even quite a lot of your stack at every round makes the “risk of ruin” unreasonably high — in the extreme, betting *all* your money on a 60-40 even-payoff coin flip ruins you on the first flip *40% of the time*. Not great.

In this example, **Full Kelly** says to bet 20% of bankroll every time. (There’d be no reason to be conservative and go half/quarter Kelly here since all the parameters and payoffs are known.). Math:

![](https://m.stacker.news/164220)

People like SBF and his effective altruist/trader peeps at Jane Street usually talked in “fractional Kelly” – i.e., bet half Kelly or quarter Kelly. SBF, as always, usually went full retarded with >1 Kelly bets; statements like being “truly risk-neutral” and having [linear utility functions](https://x.com/sbf_ftx/status/1337250704075833347) are out-of-this-world insane. (This segment in [Conservations with Tyler](https://conversationswithtyler.com/episodes/sam-bankman-fried/#:~:text=COWEN%3A%20Should,the%20other%20option.) from 2022 is *surreal*: 51-49 Russian roulette with Earth… dude says, *yes, play; over and over.*)

Grok helps me out with the exact figures and simulated estimations here:

![](https://m.stacker.news/164221)

Point being: **Half-Kelly** captures most/almost all of the upside while drastically reducing the risk — over 100 flips, Full Kelly has one-in-ten risk of finishing with less money than you started, whereas Half-Kelly has about 1.5% that risk.

## #3: APPLICATION: Kelly in the Wild, Predyx Style

*Almost rhymes.*
Den is now a degenerate gambler, having been first convinced (https://stacker.news/items/1556891 ) (and then [seduced](https://stacker.news/items/1602534)!) by the power of prediction markets.
(I find, interestingly, that they teach me a lot about bond markets and bond math in general…perhaps only because I’m reading [Wigglesworth](https://link.amazon/B0j1BrNR) now https://stacker.news/items/1588691)

I confess, most of my bets are just “feelz” – because, let’s be honest, that’s how we schtackers and Bitcoiners do everything eh? Sometimes I cross-reference with other estimates (Polymarket, clanker, or in these election times, Nate Silver). And sometimes I run my own little Kelly exercise... *which has been extremely fun and addictive and dejecting at the same time*.

**PUTIN:**

I saw the [Predyx contract](https://beta.predyx.com/market/will-vladimir-putin-remain-president-of-russia-by-july-1-2027-1778217809?ref=PREDYXTZ0UUNOP) on Putin=in office by July 1 at 93%. That seemed insane (especially as the Trump one on finishing his term -- yes, longer timeframe -- was in the mid-80s). Surely it's not *that* much of a slam dunk that dude won't die/be assassinated or leave in a coup?? 

Per mortality tables, a 74-yo has about a 2% risk of dying in the next 8 months… CAREFUL SIGGY!... Putin is “healthy” apparently, so that should pull it down a little, but he *has* lived an extremely stressful life so maybe back up to 2%.

There’s *some* [probability]([https://polymarket.com/event/russia-coup-attempt-in-2026](https://polymarket.com/event/russia-coup-attempt-in-2026)) of a coup [inside Russia](https://www.dw.com/en/how-real-is-a-coup-threat-against-russias-president/a-77098085) (say 7% over the next 8 months).

And there’s definitely a few percentage risks that he’ll be assassinated by e.g., Ukrainian drones or whatever.

Add them up, and we have a fair value of 88%. (The [Polymarket contract](https://polymarket.com/event/putin-out-before-2027) for the same timeline trades at 91%)

… plugging in the numbers in the Kelly operation above, risking 7c to make a potential profit of 93c, gives:

**\[(13.2857×0.12)−0.88]/13.2857≈ 0.05376**

FULL Kelly on my 150,000 sats Predyx portfolio is to bet 5% (8,000 sats) but I’m nowhere *near* that confident in my estimates, there’s slippage in this low-liquidity market, the Nothing-Ever-Happens is my routine strategy (https://stacker.news/items/1602534),

...and I don’t like betting against the @Team_Predyx master Undisc, so my current 1/60th Kelly seems, uh, prudent.
Maybe will add to it once @Undisciplined bids it up above/over 93% again.

***

**US 30-YEAR YIELD**

The U.S. 10y yield is at 4.9%, having fallen back markedly from its 5.3% peak three weeks ago. The 30y has moved in tandem, sitting at 5.3% currently (topped at 5.70%). So momentum is *against* this much-shorter-dated [Predyx bet](https://beta.predyx.com/market/will-the-30-year-us-treasury-yield-hit-6-in-2026-1791391546?ref=PREDYXTZ0UUNOP) that the 30y will exceed 6% in the next two months.

* Polymarket says there’s [a 6% chance]([https://polymarket.com/event/how-high-will-30-year-treasury-yield-go-before-2027/will-the-30-year-treasury-yield-hit-5pt50-before-2027-readd](https://polymarket.com/event/how-high-will-30-year-treasury-yield-go-before-2027/will-the-30-year-treasury-yield-hit-5pt50-before-2027-readd)) it’ll hit 6%.
* Using Treasury bond futures and options pricing from earlier this week (including long duration etc) the 30Y rising 69 points from here is about a 2.2 Std dev. Pretty unlikely.

Adding in the midterms and continued Iran/oil problems, plus negative public finance sentiments, I’m putting the fair value of the 30Y hitting six percent around **10%.**

bp−q=**\[(0.81×0.90)−0.10=0.736−0.10=0.64]**

Extreme upside/edge. Plug into Kelly,

![](https://m.stacker.news/164222)

Full Kelly allocation is 78%**,** so for quarter-Kelly this would be **29,000 sats.**

*Even that* is too much since I’d crash the entire Predyx contract down to about 10%, for incrementally lower payoffs. At my current share (3,202 sats at risk) I’m at 1/37th Kelly. (I could plop another 5-10k sats into this bet and still be *confidently* below tenth-Kelly.)

Will probably stack on this market over the next few days, but definitely wait for after the midterms to see what the bond market does next week.

***

Both of these illustrations are pretty good at showing how a) *your* model of reality really matters, b) the discrepancy/edge has can't be too large or too small for Kelly to help you, c) liquidity of the market you're trading in is a problem.

HOPE you enjoyed this rundown! I certainly did, and learned a bunch about the mechanics and practical employment in low-liquidity markets like Predyx.

*This is fun, guys. We’re having fun.*

items.title: Black Hole prototype ruleset
items.text:
I'm leaking The Black Hole prototype rule set. I will be presenting the protocol at Tabconf on Oct 15th.

**Description:**

The protocol uses JoinMarket’s liquidity order book and fidelity bond mechanisms, but it creates coinjoins that mimic WabiSabi’s on chain footprint.

**Design Overview:**

Coinjoin transactions that create outputs with matching values generate ephemeral tokens called “anonymity points”. Points are auctioned for sats, and the swap occurs inside a coinjoin transaction. Participants can receive points when they enter the coinjoin pool, spend from the pool, or wait inside the pool.

- Makers are liquidity providers who passively mint and sell points

- Takers are searchers who batch liquidity to mint points
- Cooperators are remixers who mint points with their own liquidity

**Point Rules:**

A transaction’s point value is determined by the sum of all inputs that were matched in their origin transactions and the sum of all outputs that are matched in the current transaction. If the number of matched inputs and the number of matched outputs in a transaction are not equal to each other, the final point value is set to the lower number.

**Maker/Taker Rules:**

- Takers must pay 57 vbytes each for up to 3 matched inputs per maker
- Takers must pay 43 vbytes for each matched output
- Takers must pay 100 vbytes for each unmatched output (43 to miners, 57 to the Maker who received it)


- Makers must pay 57 vbytes to add unmatched inputs
- Makers must pay 43 vbytes to add unmatched outputs
- Makers can’t submit two inputs each worth more than the Taker’s value target
- Makers can’t submit two inputs from the same ancestor transaction
- Makers may lock coins in fidelity bonds to improve their reputation for Taker selection


- Makers post an offer with a buying rate for points and a selling rate for points
- Makers list the maximum amount of liquidity they can provide using their 3 largest matched inputs from unique transactions
- Makers points from each origin transaction are weighted by that input’s contribution towards the Taker’s value target – Origin transactions with the least points have their value counted first
- If the Taker’s new transaction has more points than the Maker’s origin transactions, the Maker pays sats
- If the Maker’s origin transactions have more points than the Taker’s new transaction, the Maker earns sats
- Payments for points transferred atomically by adding them to one of the coinjoin outputs owned by the winner

**Cooperator Rules:**

Cooperators who pay for their own mining fees can join coordinated WabiSabi or ZeroLink rounds. Whenever mining fee rates are low enough, Cooperators are incentivized to remix UTXOs in their wallets with low points into larger rounds. These minted points can be resold later as a Maker or Taker.

- WabiSabi is flexible: It accepts any arbitrary value for inputs and outputs
- ZeroLink is strict: Rounds only accept a single standard denomination for inputs and only allows creation of a specific denomination output (input value – mining fee)

items.title: Squatting Amsterdam — Ep. 6: On the Wrong Side of the Barricade
items.text:
How yall doing stackers?

It's been a while since I posted the first and very popular series about [my squatting history in Amsterdam](https://stacker.news/items/1353355). This morning I was reminiscing some more about my early adult years in this counter culture movement and would just like to expand the series with some smaller anecdotes.

One guy, who occupies my mind frequently, was the chief of KSU Oost headquarters, the squatting unit that was based in the East of Amsterdam. As you might recall the city was broken up into multiple headquarters each governing/securing/helping the squats in their part of town. When I got my introduction course in squatting the main guy from Oost at the Pretoriusstraat told me all about how it was the done.

His name was Momo. He was originaly from Germany but spoke Dutch very well. He was a kind of hacker type who was also involved with running the squat.net servers. In spirit he felt like Morpheus from the Matrix. A mentor figure who teaches you how to hack the system. He was tall, scrawny, and wore glasses. He was a charismatic guy who often would speak at the local city council to inform the authorities on the housing situation and how the maffia was involved in it (and how the group squatted against it).

I remember one night at a squatting attempt in Oost he was spokesman. This person would lead the squat attempt, inform all the participants of the house and speak to the police when they had to confirm the break-in.

This particular break in was in a neighborhood that had partially guarded itself against squats through so-called anti-squats. Anti-squats was a legal/commercial setup in the Netherlands in which renters are recruited for temporary homes in order for them not to get squatted. You'd pay about $300/month to rent such a place. It could be really lucrative. You might get a big place in the center for a couple of years, but usually it wouldn't be such prime locations and also the stay would short.

You might say, well, if this anti-squat is so great, why not do that instead of the real squatting. The problem is you basically squander all your rental rights if you agree to the anti-squat contracts. They can throw you out with only a month notice and there's no 'huisvrede' (house peace). Huisvrede is the law that governs you, as a renter, to have the right to allow/deny whoever wants to enter your home. This means with anti-squat you frequently get visitations by the anti-squat company to inspect your place, which is really bothersome. The inspectors are usually bastards and make all kinds of notes and recommendations for the way you're living. This is not the case with squatting. With squatting you do have huisvrede and, including any eviction pending, you usually have a couple of months to find your next squat.

Anyway, so that night we squatted below some anti-squats. When the upstairs anti-squats got alarmed of the noise we made as we broke into the lower floors, they hurried to their balconies in panic to check what all the ruckus was about. When they started asking what was going on, Momo got into the conversation, and after explaining himself he said with a German accent:

> "Guys, what are you doing up there? You are on the wrong side of the barricade."

I remember that so vividly. He was trying to recruit the apparent enemy even during a squatting action. Man, I love that guy. He was very special and smart. I don't know what happened to him. Some folks said he moved to London after the squatting ban got enacted. Maybe I'll meet him again someday. I miss him. 

Now think what you may about the squatting scene in Amsterdam back in the day, and I for one have never subscribed to all of its aspects, and mainly for you (and me) this is a historic account. But there's also a point of view you can take that they weren't squatting against capitalism but against the symptoms of fiatism. Much of what I encountered in the squatting movement is in similar rebellious spirit of the Bitcoin community. 

We were all hacking against the (downstream) evils of fiat.

Hope you enjoyed this. Have a good day.

items.title: I Used to Be a Progress Man. No More (The Daily Economy, Joakim Book)
items.text:
aaaah, the attentive stackers could have seen this coming a while ago (https://stacker.news/items/1599758)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164902)

Basically a public breakup with the tech-optimistic humanprogress types. For *years*, I've struggled trying to write something for HumanProgress.org, one of the outlets I've written for a lot in the past. 

I just **can't,** anymore: it's so naive, so "*raw-raw*, look at this irrelevant techno-crappy improvement over here." \<insert *It's all fine* dog meme.>

VERY excited and grateful that I could lay out the case in print and explain, seriously and particularly, why the constant Tupy-Follett-Omary-Pooley-Morley-Crawford stuff celebrating, well, *anything* as good and improving.

I know the *exact* moment when this flip started shifting in reverse for me. (Ask me about it IRL some time.) It's been brewing for a few years.

***

> I have written something like 25 articles for [HumanProgress.org](http://humanprogress.org/), the first of which had the title “[Worldviews Are Pessimistic Because They Are Outdated.](https://humanprogress.org/a-much-needed-update-to-our-outdated-worldviews/)” I used to breathe Matt Ridley’s [*The Rational Optimist*](https://www.amazon.com/Rational-Optimist-How-Prosperity-Evolves/dp/1665102632)*,* and I’ve forced more than one unwilling family member to take [Hans Rosling](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/i-wish-that-hans-rosling-were-still-alive/)’s [Gapminder test](https://www.gapminder.org/tag/gapminder-test/) on global development.
>
> These days, I find that article’s subheading the most important bit: “When making sense of the world, we operate *on decades-old information.*” I’m gradually coming around to the view that I didn’t do my homework the first time around, and that *that* article was based “on decades-old information.”

Most of the metrics human progress-types rely on have stalled for decades. The *improvements* and amazing achievements of humanity are OLD NEWS -- they happened a long time ago. And actually, looking at the things that matter (objectively; not value judgment), it's not at all obvious that humans (in the West...) are improving much.

Actually, we might be *regressing* quite a bit. https://stacker.news/items/1601880. And we're running out of time turning that shit around https://stacker.news/items/1579572

![](https://m.stacker.news/164903)

Most obviously, the price indices people use to confidently establish how much better we are, are clearly broken. Bitcoiners know that. Economists know that. I think *even the humanprogress-type people* know that. https://stacker.news/items/1566496. But yet, they insist on trying to carve out fantastical measures in which, like, the cost of a Thanksgiving dinner non-quality-adjusted labor hours, for the increasingly fewer people working.

And if you follow the logic and evidence -- being dispassionate analysts, https://stacker.news/items/1607775, https://stacker.news/items/1606098 etc -- we're not (that much?) better off. And in quite a lot of respects, *worse* off. In the article, I point to several metrics humanprogress types always chant as amazing progress: **child mortality and working hours**. Both are correct, just outdated: child mortality hasn't improved in a generation, working hours in the most successful, wealthy/rich countries are flat for twenty years 
(They're only falling in economic basket cases like Germany, Britain, and South Korea, where government policies and green delusions have *pushed* them down... by making value-added work not worth it anymore. https://stacker.news/items/1593954)

**"The improvements of modernity are real; the timing just isn’t."**

## "in most countries there has been *no progress* in working hours over the last twenty-odd years; all the improvements come from the 1960s, ’70s, and ’80s."

> Most of the grim old days that Follett writes about in her book with that title are *from centuries ago*. Yes, compared to my ancestors who eked out a subsistence life from farming the harsh, unforgiving, and disastrously poor Nordic nature, I am miles better off. But so were my parents’ generation; and it’s not obvious that *compared to them*, my [peers and I are doing much better](https://capx.co/complaints-about-the-generational-divide-obscure-a-much-more-positive-picture). **With the obvious exception of communication tech and screens, we have the same appliances, yet can afford fewer or, at best, the same amount of stuff they could.**

Knock me down with a feather. 

***

But my real beef with these guys is that they IGNORE the obviously deteriorating and really-bad-stuff happening right before our eyes. And no, I'm not talking about climate change (I'm not retarded... https://stacker.news/items/1603339):

> In political governance and my own domains of monetary and fiscal matters, we have *definitely* regressed: the out-of-control fiscal deficits in every major country, bond yields exploding, and the [very awkward](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/the-fed-may-pause-but-inflation-wont/), [botched, post-pandemic](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/fed-admits-it-was-wrong-kind-of/) double-digit inflation are just the most obvious misdoings. Depending only a little on your ideological stance, the [ratchet effect](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/covid-19s-ratchet-effect-is-becoming-endemic/) and relentless expansion in [government spending as a share of GDP](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/historical-gov-spending-gdp?tab=line&time=1900..latest&country=JPN~USA~DEU~GBR~ISL~FIN~FRA) are a poor stand-in for “progress.” Britain, ever the role model for decline, is [hitting tax extraction levels](https://stacker.news/items/1602493) (north of 35 percent) not seen since fighting a literal world war.

> No matter what AI-fueled productivity growth may be forecast going forward, America *cannot* outgrow its $40 trillion [government debt](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/america-cant-outgrow-40-trillion-in-debt/), as Pete Earle demonstrated in a [fiscal arithmetic piece](https://civl.com/partners/growing-out-of-40-trillion-some-unpleasant-fiscal-arithmetic-4564ea48) for CiVL — to say nothing of the stagnating, struggling, and literally burning European countries stuck in a [bond yield-fiscal deficit spiral](https://ft.com/content/9b252b46-a87c-45e7-a09a-45a39ce077b8).

***

TL;DR:

> **Almost all the improvements in human welfare in the last thirty years happened in digital gadgets and communication** — and the jury is still out on whether Netflix to the masses and social media to teenagers (let alone adults) were, [on net](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/return-to-reality-the-economy-is-pivoting-amid-digital-overload/), good or bad. We’re paying for it dearly in [mental health epidemics](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/mental-health-is-in-crisis-what-is-the-answer/), broken societies, and a viciously divided polity. *Where, I repeat, is this human progress?*

The ultimate test has always been: *Would you trade places with someone in the past? What's the best time to be alive?* And the answer, to me -- having always answered, Barack Obama style, **no** + **today/tomorrow** --
is increasingly... *yes*. 

Victorian England (https://stacker.news/items/1591235) or fin-de-siècle Vienna have always been dreamy epochs for me, the lack of modern appliances and warmth and health etc aside; the post-war boomer exuberance and sense of progress is appealing; but even the very simple "20 years ago" passes the test  **It's not at all obvious to me that we're better off/live better lives today than in 2006.**

items.title: The Billionaire Bankrolling of New, Physical Print Magazines
items.text:
Over five years ago, I wrote a piece called "[An Age of Patronage](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/an-age-of-patronage/)" where I speculated how arts and research will/may work in a free world.

Basically sketching out the "value-for-value" revolution before that was cute or Lightning worked well enough for it.

## This month, I saw THREE print magazines launching/returning

**FIRST:** @asanoha and Bitcoin Art Magazine /Edition One https://stacker.news/items/1604664
This one isn't *quite* like the others -- for instance, I doubt there's a billionaire bankrolling it? -- but it's still a bet on a return to slow-form PHYSICAL MAGAZINES.

Definitely in the age of quick-hit/fast and hot takes AI slop, there's some.
Scarcity works like that, too: facing infinite generation, only the physical and human become scarce (https://stacker.news/items/1603955, https://stacker.news/items/1608788, https://stacker.news/items/1604664)

**SECOND:** LIFE magazine, a mainstay of 20th-century America, [is back](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/28/business/media/life-magazine-karlie-kloss.html). From that NYT article:

> The iconic magazine, known for its red-box logo and devotion to visual storytelling, will start publishing again next month as a quarterly print magazine.

*This*:

> It enters a fractured media landscape that is worlds away from the publication’s midcentury heights of acclaim, before the internet, social media and artificial intelligence upended the business model of magazine publishing.
> Daniel Okrent, who was the editor of Life magazine from 1992 to 1996, said that despite the value of the Life logo and the quality of the content, it was “a constantly unprofitable magazine” throughout history.

Also: run as a passion project/vanity thing for [small-time millionaire](https://www.celebritynetworth.com/richest-celebrities/models/karlie-kloss-net-worth/) and supermodel Karlie Kloss. Ruins Den's billionaire trend? No: husband is a [multibillionaire](https://www.eonline.com/news/1434962/inside-billionaire-josh-kushner-karlie-kloss-private-world). Funzies.

Also, importantly: NOT littered with ads. (Makes sense, since ad revenue isn't bankrolling them ANYWAY)

> The issue will come out on Nov. 23 as a large-format, 250-page print magazine retailing for $45, combining news photography with long-form journalism. There are no traditional print ads; instead the first issue is sponsored by Rivian and Figma.

says Wikipedia for why it closed its doors 25 years ago:

![](https://m.stacker.news/165194)

***

**THIRD:** Works in Progress.

Been seeing this a lot in my feed in recent weeks. (I imagine the algos heavily favor something you've visited/searched for recently) https://stacker.news/items/1591235, https://stacker.news/items/1598977, https://stacker.news/items/1601320

https://x.com/WorksInProgMag/status/2115617294005284869

No slop, *craft* in making beautiful things -- *and* important content.

The entire project is bankrolled by Stripe // Stripe Publishing and ultimate *their*owners, Patrick and John Collison et al.

***

It's *very* interesting to see this semi-/fake-capitalistic development, with art and storytelling and journalism be portrayed and worked on passionately by REAL and SERIOUS people, that looks and behaves like any other capitalist enterprise -- just *won't* be profit-oriented or ever aspire to making a profit.

## They're in it for the tech...

or rather, the humanity of it. The changing society. The craft and beauty and *deep meaning*.

I live this trend. And apparently, *sic semper salvatores*:

https://x.com/CharlesCMann/status/2118334333782012086

## All successful journalistic efforts were similarly "bankrolled by wealthy eccentrics"?

Yeah, I dunno. *But what did the rich ever do for us?!*

The recent anti-billionaire campaigns channeled their energy incorrectly. It's not that [the "rich" need to finance](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/an-age-of-patronage/) failing programs like Medicare, or fat, lazy Californians' health problems. They should just build shit, bankroll artists, be \_patrons\_ to us creative peeps... and churches and architecture and all the other beautiful things in human/western civ. 

## "patronage is “the tribute which opulence owes to genius.” --Edmund Burke

> If you were wealthy, **it was your moral obligation to give back to the community** – not merely by improving the lot of the poor or renovating your local church but also by supporting artists and intellectuals.

Interesting future ahead of us. Huuuuge if true.

items.title: This is my last Christmas as Santa Claus.
items.text:
Yes, it hurts just as much as I imagined it would. My daughter has reached the age where the magic comes to an end more and more questions, fewer friends who still believe in magic, and more friends confirming that it’s actually the parents who place the gifts under the tree every December 25th.

Playing the role of Santa this Christmas season was spectacular; the excitement, the happiness, the smile, and the look in my daughter’s eyes every December 25th are truly priceless. Buying gifts on the sly and stashing them away in secret, strategic spots is so much fun. I’m open to new traditions, though I’m also a bit scared and nervous about the next stages of her childhood.

I have previously made posts in which I’ve been chronicling this journey into the world of fantasy

[I managed to find the right answer to my daughter's questions about Santa Claus](https://stacker.news/items/1253270/r/bief57)

[Does Santa Claus commit labor exploitation?Questions from my 8 year old daughter](https://stacker.news/items/996626/r/bief57)

[Does the tooth fairy print money? Questions my 8-year-old daughter asks me.](https://stacker.news/items/990421/r/bief57)

About two months ago, I was walking down the street with my daughter when, out of the blue, she asked me: "Do parents pay Santa Claus to bring the gifts?"

I stayed silent, pretending I hadn’t heard, while I thought about how to respond. I considered making up a lie—an interesting story, something to keep his belief in magic alive—but then I remembered he’s nine years old; by this age, most children in the middle years of primary school no longer believe in fairy tales. I also thought about the risk of bullying, and the fact that living in a fictional world isn’t exactly healthy when reality can be so cruel. So, I simply replied, "Yes, parents have to pay." My intention was to spark some doubt and critical thinking—to plant the seed of reality without being too blunt. He immediately burst into tears, and we had to sit down on the sidewalk. I shed a few tears myself and asked him what was making him sad. He began asking questions: "How much money do they get?" "So, you’re the ones who choose the gifts?" "Back before bank transfers existed, did they pay with checks?" I cracked a joke—"Does that mean Santa Claus is basically a toy delivery service?"—and we both managed a little laugh.

I wonder if I’ve lied to him about other things, and if he suspects that the same is true when it comes to the Tooth Fairy.

We had a pleasant conversation—at least it was for me, and I hope it was for her, too. She told me that what saddened her most was that reality isn’t as fun as the idea of a magical man arriving in December on a flying sleigh to hand out toys. She also used the phrase "everything is a business" when I confirmed that, yes, we actually give money to Santa.

I wondered why we parents create these magical stories, and I told her that it’s a tradition meant to encourage the imagination. I shared that when I was a child, I enjoyed it myself; eventually, I figured out the truth, but I still helped preserve the innocence of my younger sisters while they were still little. I wanted to do the same for her, because love is the closest thing there is to magic. I explained that this is why not everyone follows this tradition—in fact, some religions even forbid it. I also explained that every person or culture constructs its own fantasy world; these can be rooted in doing good, or conversely, in causing harm—for instance, through practices like Santería or witchcraft (which are quite common here in Venezuela).

I’m left with a bitter taste of disappointment and sadness, but it was time; he still believes there’s a fellow named Saint Nicholas who delivers toys at the request of parents—maybe next year he’ll get to know "Saint Amazon" (just a joke).



Christmas 2025

items.title: EXTROPY — the 1988–1996 archive
items.text:
Extropy - "the vaccine for future shock" was a precursor to the Cypherpunk Mailing List and home to many of the ideas that went on to be discussed by that community.

This (AI generated website) has digitized the contents of a great number of their issues. There are some great articles in here including an article on [exercise and longevity by Fran Finney](https://extropy.agoraops.org/issues/09/exercise-and-longevity/), an article about [digital cash and privacy by Hal Finney](https://extropy.agoraops.org/issues/10/protecting-privacy-with-electronic-cash/), and something about [Creole Physics and the Credit Theory of Identity](https://extropy.agoraops.org/issues/10/mark-miller-interview-pt1/) by Dave Krieger, among many others.

You could do worse than to spend some time reading these.

What to do about natural-dividend windfalls is a theme on Den's mind this year https://stacker.news/items/1589657 https://stacker.news/items/1565551 https://stacker.news/items/1515430

![](https://m.stacker.news/165141)

> Today, the Alaska Permanent Fund has assets of $88 billion. It’s not as big as Norway’s oil fund, which we [discussed](https://www.netinterest.co/p/the-biggest-investor-in-the-world) some time ago, but it’s the closest America has to a sovereign wealth fund. Each year, the state is allowed to draw 5% from the fund to finance government services and to pay a dividend to residents. This year, eligible residents will each receive a check for $1,200.

But interestingly, at first it consisted *only* of bonds -- even though this was, in principle, a perpetual fund lasting looong into the future https://stacker.news/items/1609745

> . In 1999, its mandate was broadened to allow a 5% allocation to alternative investments and, in 2004, the fund made its first foray into hedge funds. \[Those] were made through a fund-of-funds program. Alaska hired three managers to select hedge funds on its behalf but performance was disappointing. In the ten years through to 2016, those hedge funds generated a 3.4% annualized return

How about this for epic alpha investing? Nine years, 6.7% annualized return *and no down years*. Sexy:

> The shift in approach paid off. Alaska now allocates to 18 managers, accounting for 8% of its total portfolio. When markets slid in 2022, the hedge fund part of its portfolio was up about 8%. In the nine years since the restructuring, the average annualized return of the hedge fund portfolio has been 6.7% with no down years and a low correlation to overall markets.

![](https://m.stacker.news/165147)

## "The problem, though, is that “the more money we push into absolute return, the harder it is to get that really special return because the good funds are capacity constrained.”

**I'm sure that's why Undisc can't rule the ROI league at** @Team_Predyx **anymore!**

THANKFULLY,

> Perhaps Millennium has an answer to that.
> When Alaska first invested, Millennium was a $35 billion fund; it is now knocking on the door of $100 billion. Its return in October was [weak](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-03/major-hedge-funds-mostly-lose-in-nowhere-to-hide-october?srnd=undefined), down 2.3%, but that sits within its risk tolerance limits and compared with other funds, it could have been worse. How it performs in November, when many funds have struggled, will be key.

...but, "to see what Millennium is up to," we need to bypass a paywall. And Den is cheap (poor? lazy?!) so there's no Net Interest subscription!

We shall never find out what the secret Millennium hedge fund sauce is.

items.title: A Lodging for Wayfaring Men Book Club: Chapter 3
items.text:
*Welcome to the sixth week of our book club reading* A Lodging for Wayfaring Men. *We're reading one chapter every two weeks, so we'll today be discussing Chapter 3 (but in between-weeks we are having a look at the essays in Appendix A. They are short and accessible).*

*You can find the book club reading schedule here:* https://stacker.news/items/1582413

***

The story of people who are trying to build unstoppable, unregulated markets on the internet is really cool. Unfortunately, Rosenberg is not doing the best job of it. I often feel like he glosses over the most interesting parts and includes quite a lot of stuff that doesn't add much to the story at all.

For instance, I'm not quite sure what the purpose of the biomedical peptides "Brain Flush" storyline is. Sure, that's cool, too -- but why do the freedom market people also need to be inventing a thing that cures you from all your emotional baggage? And then there's the free love stuff.

I can see how it all kind of connects in the theme of regulation impeding humans from being as fully developed as they can be, but it's too widespread to do justice to any single storyline. I would love to see more character development or even discussion of ideas, the characters just don't need to be saving the world along quite so many verticals.

Still, Rosenberg doesn't fail to include a number of interesting points that made me stop and think. The greatest of these, at least in this chapter, was this:

> But the Internet opened up a virgin territory for us. A territory that is a hell of a lot harder to control than a geographic territory. And because the basic structure of cyberspace is distributed, not centralized, we have a built-in advantage.
>
> What we are doing is a natural progression of the digital revolution. What the governments are trying to do is to reroute the digital revolution, against its nature, to serve their desire for centralized dominion.
>
> "The Internet must be protected. We can't let it become a tool of the old territorial rulers. So, we are building a center of private interactions, where rulers cannot intrude. It was a strange moment when several of us looked around and said to each other, 'Oh my God, we can't let this opportunity pass, and we are the adults. We have to step in adn see to this; we're here, we're able, and it has fallen to us."

I really strongly believe in this vision for the internet, and since I've been reading some of the archives of the Cypherpunks Mailing List lately, it doubly resonated. It seems that using the Internet as the home of truly free markets was developed in tandem with the internet itself. At the first meeting of the Cypherpunks they played a game that simulated using the internet for exactly this purpose https://stacker.news/items/1609744/r/Scoresby.

The internet has been in full flower for many decades and bitcoin has been around for almost two, but for me at least, the question of whether such unregulated markets exist is still unclear https://stacker.news/items/1608631/r/Scoresby.

So, what do you think: has the internet fallen to regulation, surveillance and control, or is there still hope that we can play the crypto anarchy game for real?

# How is this battle for the internet going? Are we winning? Or are the scales tipping in favor of the government?

items.title: Javokhir Sindarov vs Gukesh Dommaraju: Chess Championship (FIDE, Peter Svidler)
items.text:
Short interview with Peter Svidler, a legend of the game who, himself, challenged for the title in the early 2000s. While no longer an active player (mostly just a coach or commentator these days,) at his current, inactive, rating he'd qualify as **#42** in the world.

Here he discusses the recent form of the two championship contenders *and* comments on their respective style. Actually, he says, "style" doesn't make much sense for these youngsters who came off age in the era of computers... having practiced with and analyzed games with them since forever.

> People who reach this level are pretty much *always* universal... so talking about stylistic preferences for someone playing for the world championship was KIND OF ridiculous because they could do everything.
> but *this* generation of players seem to be a lot more concrete -- and a lot less hung up on the things which were obsessions for players of previous generations: things like "sound" positional play. 
>
> It's not that they *can't* play positional chess, of course they can, but their formative years were spent working with computers and that very much changes how they view the game. Because if there's one thing that computers teach you, time and time again, it is that **a lot more is affordable; a lot more is defensible; a lot more is possible**, if you can just calculate really, really cleanly.

## "It's a lot more natural to them to play dynamic chess than to play positional chess"

**What will be the key factors in the championship game?**

Openings won't matter... everyone is extremely well prepared, and everybody plays the same openings.

Psych and mentality, keeping yourself (and your emotions) in check(!) will matter.

> 60% \[Javokhir] is already very high; even with the kind of year that Gukesh has had, going higher than 55-45 isn't justifiable. Gukesh is still a very strong player, it's still a very specific format. **I'm sort of willing to go 55-45 Sindarov** but I don't think I'm willing to go higher.

Also, checking in on the Predyx odds:
