items.title: Blok's Stock Review: Portland General Electric Company (POR)
items.text:
***USD/BTC = $75,814***
 ***Block 974,944***

## Today's Stock: Portland General Electric Company (POR)

![](https://m.stacker.news/165155)

Portland General Electric is a regulated electric utility serving Portland and the northern Willamette Valley in Oregon. It generates, buys, transmits and distributes power to homes and businesses. 

## My Thoughts 💭

One share costs 60,609 sats ($45.95). It pays $2.205 a year in dividends, 2,908 sats a share, so it would take about 21 years of dividends to break even on one share at that price. The P/E is 20.0, a 20 year payback on earnings. There is no payback at all on free cash flow because free cash flow is negative. Let's review the fundamentals to determine if this stock is worth spending sats on.

## PE:

![](https://m.stacker.news/165157)

P/E 20.0 TTM on earnings of $273M. Simply Wall St calls it good value against the peer average of 22.2 and against its fair P/E of 20.8, but expensive against the electric utilities industry average of 19.5. The price sits right on my rule 3 line of under 20, not below it.

## Expected Growth:

![](https://m.stacker.news/165159)

Earnings are forecast to grow 14.35 percent a year and revenue 7.4 percent a year. EPS is expected to grow 39 percent over the next 3 years against 19 percent for the industry. Forecast ROE rises to 9.3 percent from 6.3 percent today. Add the 4.8 percent dividend yield to the growth and the projected total return is about 19 percent a year. That clears my 15 percent Bitcoin bear hurdle but not the 30 percent bull hurdle.

## Revenues and expenses:


![](https://m.stacker.news/165160)


Revenue $3.55B TTM with net income of $273M, a 7.68 percent net margin. Cash from operations is $959M a year, but free cash flow is negative $416M a year and Simply Wall St calls the trend alarming. Rule 5 fails. A utility pouring cash into the grid still has to show positive free cash flow sooner or later.

## Balance Sheet:

![](https://m.stacker.news/165161)

Total debt $5.43B against cash and short term investments of just $69M. Debt to equity is 125.4 percent and interest is covered only 2.1 times by earnings. Normal leverage for a utility, but rules 1 and 4 fail outright on my sheet.

## Dividend:

![](https://m.stacker.news/165162)

Yield 4.8 percent on $2.205 a share a year, which passes rule 2 with room. The payout ratio is 90 percent of earnings though, so rule 6 fails, and Simply Wall St says the dividend is not well covered by earnings or free cash flows. The next payment is $0.55 a share, ex date December 22, 2026, pay date January 15, 2027. Share count is also rising, a buyback yield of negative 6.5 percent, which dilutes the holder while the dividend goes out the door.

## Bitcoin per share:

None. POR holds no BTC on its balance sheet.

## Ownership breakdown:


![](https://m.stacker.news/165163)


Institutions hold 99.5 percent, insiders 0.435 percent. The top 25 shareholders own about 71 percent, with BlackRock the largest at 15.7 percent.

## Leadership:

![](https://m.stacker.news/165164)

CEO Maria Pope has run the company since October 2017. Her total compensation is $7.58M, below the $8.42M average for companies of similar size, and Simply Wall St flags no excessive pay concern. Rule 7 passes.

## Blok's 9 rules: 3 of 9

1. ❌ Debt $5.43B with a debt to equity ratio of 125.4 percent
2. ✅ Dividend yield 4.8 percent
3. ⚠️ P/E 20.0 sits right on the line, not under 20
4. ❌ Cash $69M against debt of $5.43B
5. ❌ Free cash flow is negative $416M
6. ❌ Payout ratio 90 percent
7. ✅ CEO pay $7.58M is below the similar size average of $8.42M
8. ✅ Energy, a regulated electric utility
9. ⚠️ Projected return near 19 percent clears the 15 percent bear hurdle only

## Lyn's Lens:

The first pillar passes at the door. POR is a profitable company with hard regulated assets and real earnings. Her entry math for mid teens growth plus a near 5 percent yield supports roughly 25x to 30x earnings, and on trailing EPS of $2.29 that implies about $57 to $69. The $45.95 price works on earnings with room to spare. Cash is where her lens turns. Free cash flow is negative, the dividend is not covered by it, and the balance sheet carries real leverage. Lyn's Lens says the price works on earnings, not on cash flow.

## Closing take

While I am a fan of investing in utilities I think buying and holding 60k worth of sats should perform better than this utility company. The high leverage and low FCF makes me think this is a dead but essential company. Investors won’t get rich holding this but it will take a long grind to get the initial investment back while inflation will continue to erode the value of the dollar. This is a pass for me!

Price context: $45.95 sits near the low end of its range between $43.26 and $54.62 over the past year, down about 4 percent in that year. Simply Wall St puts its cash flow value at $46.60 and the analyst consensus target at $52.27.

items.title: OpenBitcoin.com: A new bitcoin block explorer with guides tools and games
items.text:
I have been building a bitcoin block explorer and I feel it's good enough to show:

[https://openbitcoin.com](https://openbitcoin.com)

The site runs its own hardware, bitcoin node and address index. No third-party blockchain API used.

Inside the site:

- Explorer: blocks, transactions and addresses at root-level URLs. (very important, a feature I always wanted with other explorers, a quick easy way to query an address) For example you can type openbitcoin.com/block_number_here or openbitcoin.com/txid_here or openbitcoin.com/address_here to load the page instantly without visiting the site to use the search bar :)

- Node census (openbitcoin.com/nodes): reachable nodes counted by my own P2P crawler, 8,958 nodes from 92 countries last run.

- Rich list (openbitcoin.com/rich-list): top 10,000 addresses and balance distributions.

- Prices: spot price as a median of three exchanges, with a quick conversion tool on the front page.

- Tools: fee calculator, address validator, message verifier, QR generator, and key tools built to be downloaded and run offline.

- Guides: on confirmations, UTXOs, self-custody, stuck transactions and more. Newbie friendly.

- Games (openbitcoin.com/games): three arcade games built on real bitcoin mechanics, stack blocks, clear a mempool backlog, and a slot machine that plays the actual odds of guessing a private key.

The website is open source. What stays private is my server's operational layer.

Would appreciate any feedback, happy to contribute to the community.

items.title: Chess-November Continues: Introducing the Total Chess Championship
items.text:
Yes, I'm back making *another* chess market. And *yes*, there's *another* major chess tournament this month.

## The chess world is insane: drama everywhere.

Meaning, importantly, that Javokhir and Gukesh are *not* participating. (duh) https://stacker.news/items/1610211

This format is sort of more along the lines of what Magnus wanted FIDE to turn toward, with a mix of time controls and an open tournament sort of situation rather than the grueling one-on-one matches the world championship consists of https://stacker.news/items/1608324

So, our beloved chess No. 1 and GOAT is here, pwning it off.

![](https://m.stacker.news/165197)

![](https://m.stacker.news/165198)

![](https://m.stacker.news/165199)

I kind of *don't* quite understand all the nuances of the format (but as you follow along the tourney, it usually makes more sense!!) https://stacker.news/items/1609473

...and if it doesn't, I shall be around to help! (or, you know, just ask your favorite AI; what do I care -.-)

***

ANYWAY:

There's **24** players in the tournament, about half with roughly *0%* chance of winning. I couldn't be arsed funding/specifying *all* potential winners, so I just included the tops/my favs -- and shoved all the others into, well, "Others."

Since we're all degenerate gamblers here, I thoroughly expect "Team Hans" (https://stacker.news/items/1609473?commentId=1609678) to bid up his poor chances (currently at 7%) to higher than that. I launched it with these probabilities (and then added some neat bids myself so the market doesn't look so sad!)

- **Magnus**: 30%
- **Nodirbek**: 20%
- **Pragg**: 10%
- **Niemann**: 5%
- **Others** (including Rapport, Arjun, Fabiano, Nepo, Anish, Shak) = 35%

Magnus is \_obviously\_ the top favorite in every tournament he plays, but what's so cool about elite chess in the ano 2026 is that *on a good day* any of these guys can beat him in a single game or two... *especially* in the shorter time controls where the youngsters (Nodirbek, Alireza, Niemann etc) definitely have a good chance.

![](https://m.stacker.news/165201)

## Go forth and bet, my chessy friends

**And let's look forward to a wonderful month of even-more wonderful chess!**

items.title: There's 0.2024 BTC hidden inside Pierre Noizat's book (French edition)
items.text:
## [L'énergie, face cachée de la monnaie](https://www.kobo.com/us/en/ebook/l-energie-face-cachee-de-la-monnaie)

Nobody has cracked it in 2 years, but recently, we started to receive a lot of emails asking for clues.
Initially, 7 clues were released, but even with frontier AI tools, the wallet still hasn't been drained.

recap and more clues below👇

![](https://m.stacker.news/165108)

***

First clue: “A picture is worth a thousand words, but eight pictures are worth fourteen.”

2. Then there are 2 Olympic years.
3. Department of origin.
4. 2 in the table of contents.
5. 2 in a chapter that deals with a central theme of the book.
6. Une traduction en anglais est en cours.
7. In the end, decentralized networks always prevail.

This isn't a clue but a clarification that could be useful: how does one go from a 24-word mnemonic passphrase to a Bitcoin address?

More specifically, how does one find the private key of an address from a mnemonic phrase?

***

Seven clues were revealed between August 15 and September 26, 2024.
As of now, that has not been enough, despite the shrewdness of the bitcoiners.

There will therefore be 7 additional clues (numbered 8 to 14): one every Thursday until December 19 inclusive, then 3 clues on

All the words are found on the normalized list [http://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039/](http://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039/).

The first 21 words to find (in the book) are in French and the last 3 in English. Then replace each of the 21 French words with the one of the same rank in the english.txt list

To verify that you have correctly found the first 23 words, the word staff (1697) can be used in the 24th position to form a valid mnemonic phrase compatible with wallets that allow the use of 24-word phrases, including Blockstream's wallet.

In fact, any of these 8 words can be used in the 24th position as the checksum word:
alien
detect
flip
gas
organ
peasant
staff
trigger

All you need to do then is replace it with the 24th word (which is NOT one of the 8 words above) and calculate the “seed”.

The first 14 words are contained in the book's images, taken in order. The words million, minutes, and opinions are not part of the solution because they are used multiple times in the images or in the plural.
The 13th and 14th words are on the cover.

The Olympic years are linked to the author's biography (15th and 16th words). Be careful, there is false information on certain unreliable sites.
The 17th word is linked to the author's name.

The 18th and 19th words are in the summary.

The words in the 22nd, 23rd, and 24th positions form a slogan used in 2024 by a brand known worldwide, inspired by a title from the group Tomorrow x Together.

***

Get the book here:
[https://konsensus.net/books/?b=lenergie-face-cachee-de-la-monnaie-2](https://konsensus.net/books/?b=lenergie-face-cachee-de-la-monnaie-2)
(also available in English)

Curious to see who's going to crack it

`Burns and McDonnell has completed Missouris largest membrane bioreactor system as part of the city of Republics $145 million wastewater infrastructure program, about 1,916 BTC at todays rate ($145,000,000 / $75,673).`

The upgraded Republic Water Reclamation Facility now treats 5 million gallons per day. The expansion is a first of its kind treatment solution in Missouri and helps the city handle compliance challenges and prepare for future growth.

The $145 million program also includes peak wet weather improvements and three collection system projects.` The city financed it through direct allocations, state revolving fund loans and revenue bonds. `Republic has been working with Burns and McDonnell on a water and wastewater master plan since 2017.

The project used progressive design build, a first for Republic. When early estimates came in over budget, the team used value engineering to bring the price down while keeping the original treatment goals.

"Working as one team helped us respond to cost pressures, plan construction around ongoing operations and prepare staff to operate the new systems," said Alli White, operations manager at Burns and McDonnell.

`The water market stays hot. Burns and McDonnell is bullish on water going into 2027, and McCarthy Building Cos. president of water Jaren Murphy told Construction Dive that almost every large municipality now has a billion dollar plus capital improvement plan in motion.`

I think the water market will continue to be hot!

items.title: Why Milei's Chainsaw Revolution Required Restraint
items.text:
> **Critics are divided as Javier Milei takes gradual, constrained steps toward the radical free market he campaigned on.**
>
> In December 2023, as the sound of a chainsaw echoed through Buenos Aires, Javier Milei swept into the Casa Rosada, and pro-market Austrian School economists cheered his victory. Nearly three years later, many libertarians are disappointed. They keep asking themselves: Did they vote for [Rothbard](https://mises.org/profile/murray-n-rothbard), only to get another central planner?
>
> He campaigned on a platform that was not merely reformist but explicitly abolitionist. He promised to end the Central Bank, dollarize the economy, and rein in the interventionist state. The Central Bank of Argentina (BCRA) still opens its doors every morning. The government did not [lift restrictions](https://www.elibrary.imf.org/view/journals/002/2025/219/article-A001-en.xml) on moving foreign currencies until April 2025. To an orthodox libertarian, all of this might still look like central planning.
>
> That criticism has divided free-market thinkers, including Austrian economists. Hans-Hermann Hoppe, for example, has criticized Milei for not acting radically enough. [Milei responded sharply in an interview](https://x.com/LibertarianDuty/status/1867202040742522933) and accused Hoppe of lacking sufficient knowledge of monetary economics. Milei argued that the demands for immediate change ignore important risks, such as hyperinflation.
>
> Milei believes that poorly timed good policy can lead to the worst outcome. He believes that the path to a free market must begin with ending persistent budget deficits, not lifting capital controls. He hopes this approach will advance his political agenda while limiting political tensions and inflation risk.
>
> Milei’s background as a macroeconomist explains his thinking. In this sense, his approach is technocratic because he prioritizes the economic conditions needed to achieve his free-market goals, even if that requires more nuance than his ideological promises.
>
> [**...read more at thedailyeconomy.org**](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/why-mileis-chainsaw-revolution-required-restraint/)

items.title: In Search of Freedom: Life, Death, and Sovereignty in the Himalaya
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/164458)

*I’m sitting in a dusty hotel room in Kathmandu, attempting to call a Spanish airline about my missing luggage.*
*“We’ll have to email our ground staff contractor,” they say.*
*I try to protest. “My trek starts tomorrow!”*
*“Please check your email later today, sir.”*
*I listen to the click of the agent hanging up the phone.*

The hotel is nestled precisely in the middle of Thamel, the tourist district with its colourful flags, rooftop gardens, and too-narrow streets. There is plenty to do in the capital, but after three days of chasing my lost bag in a Kafkaesque system of virtual shrugs and missed callbacks, my energy wanes. I am trapped in the antipresent, unable to visit any tourist attractions, only capable of reconnecting to the hotel WiFi to refresh my emails for the 800th time in the hope of news. With nothing but time, I feel utterly trapped.

During a 2018 volunteering trip to Nepal, I waited for my opportunity to walk the Annapurna Circuit: a two-week hiking route crossing high paths and winding through tiny Buddhist villages. Instead, I got a call to fly back to the UK. My father had been diagnosed with bowel cancer, and it was terminal. He was the one who introduced me to hiking, taught me to be patient when faced with another false peak, to understand the swirling patterns of clouds, to clean my kit, to be prepared for sudden change, to appreciate in the silence of the wilderness, to be present. Near the end, we talked a lot about hiking.

“When you see a mountain,” he said, “think of me.”
I can’t remember what I said in return.

It took eight years to get back to Nepal — grief, travel, COVID, relocation, work, money, rule changes, and procrastination saw to that. After all my posturing about being an advocate for freedom, living my life exactly how I wanted, my fear of closure held me back. I wouldn’t gain perspective until I’d seen those mountains again.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164459)

*Finally, after another two-day delay, I take the first steps of my 18-day trek. The Manang Valley bathes in bright sunlight. We pass apple orchards and fields of buckwheat as we climb to Lower Pisang, but after nearly a week stuck in the hotel, I feel like I could run up the path for hours. I’m not doing this alone; there are ten in my group — other travellers looking for answers in the hills. We get to know each other in the brief moments when we’re not gasping for breath in the thinning air.*

That night, I fire up my Kindle and read [*The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas*](https://shsdavisapes.pbworks.com/f/Omelas.pdf). It’s one of my all-time favourites, a short story that’s more of a thought experiment. Ursula Le Guin presents a Utopian society of harmony, peace, and joy. In Omelas, life is wonderful for every resident except one: a miserable child, suffering alone in a dungeon. Most residents can ignore the one person whose incarceration guarantees their joy and freedom, but the few who can’t leave the citadel forever.

Maybe it’s hubris, but I’ve always considered myself one of those who ‘walk away’. I’ve been willing to give up convenience to claw back some of the sovereignty I’d lost through a corporate job and living in a mediocre London suburb. And here I was on a legendary remote hiking route, perhaps not scaling peaks, but at least challenging myself, climbing higher than I’ve ever been.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164462)

*The nights are cold at 4000m above sea level, and my wardrobe is more suited to the Spanish summer than sub-zero temperatures. As we hike farther up, across metal suspension bridges and past well-insulated herds of yaks, I wear my father’s old gear — a down vest and the bright red* *waterproof. It’s not a homage; it’s purely practical. Still, it gives me some kind of connection.*

I feel him silently judging me for walking the ‘tourist trail’. He always had to plan the route and bring every bit of kit himself, while a Nepalese porter carries my luggage strapped directly to their forehead. He would also have loved seeing the world’s highest peaks up close and listening to the guides' explanations of the dangers, the routes, the climbers. We all live the battle of comfort vs sovereignty.

The ‘tea house’ hotels in the Manang valley have a few more mod cons than expected. Some even have hot showers. But today, the power for the whole village is out. As the sun sets, my roommate and I read by the light of our headtorches.

Before the trip, I’d just finished reading *The Gulag Archipelago*, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn’s brutal account of the anti-freedoms of Communist Russia. That night, I search for a quote that jumped off the page when I read it: ‘All those years in our cells and our huts, the state’s electricity had seared our souls, and now, darkness was bliss.’ Sometimes, our only freedom comes through stoic minimalism and absence. I turned off my reading light and listened to the darkness.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164463)

*I’m in bed with a worsening cold. The lack of doctors and pharmacies doesn’t seem so quaint when you are coughing up your lungs. The 5,416m Thorong La Pass plays on my mind, and I struggle to sleep. It’s not just me; another member of the group has a virus, and most of the others are blowing their runny noses in the dry mountain air. We take each day slowly, climbing 500m in altitude, and putting one foot in front of the other. There aren’t any other options: turning back involves walking too, and I don’t like going backwards.*

By this point, we’ve walked 80km or so. [Karl Bushby](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8rz38jr50go) has just finished walking 50,000km after circumnavigating the globe by foot. I watched a video on his trip just before setting off on mine, and I was most impressed by the fact he had no desire to break records, no charity campaign, no press team. “Every fibre of my being,” he says, “every day, has been what I'm doing right now.”

Along the way, between icy paths and sneezes, I hit upon the idea that walking is trustless. That’s why it is so freeing to Karl Bushby and to all of us. You don’t rely on anyone or anything else. It is the rhythm of taking one step at a time. Sometimes things go as expected; sometimes they don't. But freedom is not about control. It depends on adapting to your surroundings and being in sync with the path. Each day, the tea houses serve another group of foreigners. Monks in the small temples perform another ceremony, another meditation. The kitchens produce another hundred plates of dal bhat, accompanied by ginger tea for the sniffling guests. The sun rises over snowy peaks again.

One of the guys in our group walked to Everest Base Camp more than 20 years ago. Things were quite primitive back then. He told me the soundtrack of those two weeks was the constant *thunk* of cattle bells. That was his rhythm, his surroundings. He bought a heavy metal bell in a Kathmandu market at the end of his trip and still displays it proudly in his New Jersey house.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164464)

*It’s 4 am and -15℃ on the day we climb over the pass and down the other side. Lines of headtorches light the steep path up, and the snow crunches under boots fitted with temporary metal spikes. The path ahead is backed up because a girl from another group has fainted. Her partner attempts to carry her up on piggyback, but stops after just a few steps.*

*As we wait for the last members of our party to arrive, we hop from foot to foot to keep warm. Frank, a German realtor who lives in Cape Town, excitedly tells us he has the WiFi password for a teahouse we’ve just passed. ‘Who cares?’ I think. ‘You’ve flown all the way here to cross this pass, and you’ve gotten up in the dark to do it. Why do you need WiFi?’*

Later, after the girl who collapsed has passed us riding on a yak, after we’ve taken our photos at the top, and after we’ve descended to 3,800 meters and bathed in the sun of the afternoon, I reflect on Frank and his need for WiFi passwords. Yes, we are all plugged into our digital worlds, but if you can’t spend a few hours away from it, are you really free at all?

I think about the amount of time I spent that day completely disconnected, staring at the contrast of birds of prey crossing white peaks and soaring up into a blue sky. Why do we struggle to think beyond the next unit of time? The next breath, photo, coffee break, the next day, the next WiFi access point. Why do we need to extract immediate value from our physical world?

I can’t always rein in my differences from the group. Not everyone has waited eight long years to reconnect with their father by climbing a Nepalese mountain. This is every fibre of my being, not just a social media photo op. My father would have loved to build a homestead, to fix machines, grow cattle, and walk the land, but he chose a secure life so his children could do that.

The next days we pass through small towns celebrating *Dashain* — a time for families, giving thanks, and taking stock. We stay with a local family and experience life in a small town; while we eat set meals and walk to a strict schedule, it feels like all the Nepalis around us are making their own choices.

We watch old ladies harvesting millet and corn. Heavy machinery continues to shift the earth of roads and riverbanks affected by landslides. We see new entrepreneurs opening restaurants, tea houses, and local stores. I speak to Ram, one of our guides, who is working through the festival period to put his kids through college in Japan. Everyone must hustle to improve their lot because saving in Rupees is futile. Even with remittances from those working abroad, Nepal is constantly playing catch-up. Everyone is building a better life here; no one expects it to be easy.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164466)

*My final day is spent in Kathmandu. A few of us travel to Durbar Square to see the world’s only living goddess. The Kumari is a young girl selected from a northern village. There are strict physical and mental tests as well as a birthdate that matches specific astrological criteria. She is taken from her parents to live in an opulent palace, where her feet may never touch the ground below. If she sheds a drop of blood, she is cast out into the realm of the mortals and is replaced by a new Kumari. Hindus and Buddhists alike come to see her, hoping to be blessed by one of her three daily appearances at her palace window. The current Kumari is just three years old. After waiting an hour for her to appear, I feel like her nervous little wave is an anticlimax. The crowd still gasps.*

Later, it hits me that she is the living embodiment of the child in *The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas*. Instead of being tortured or in pain, she is doted on. She has expensive gowns, extravagant makeup, a team of handlers, tutors, and adoring fans, but she is cursed. Her childhood is stolen, and she is imprisoned to bring others luck, joy, and religious harmony. She cannot play, shout, hide, misbehave, cry, laugh, or neglect her duties. She cannot walk where she pleases. To tourists, the Kumari is a sweet anomaly, a curious tradition. To Nepalis, she is a living goddess. Almost everyone is happy with this arrangement.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164460)

I went to Nepal to reconnect with emotions I had long since buried. Curiously, I saw glimpses of freedom instead of apparitions of my father. Sometimes I saw them in the hawks cruising high above, sometimes in the industrious lives of locals, and sometimes in the restrictions of those trapped in digital worlds or religious constructs.

If there is one thing I learned on this journey across the Annapurna mountains, it is that freedom is gained one step at a time. You have to know which direction you are heading, and you must understand what you are leaving behind.

items.title: My daughter’s tenacious spirit
items.text: Travelled to the end of the world (aka Pasir Ris), but I wasn’t deterred by the long commuting time. See, I went prepared because I had brought along the Berries textbook. On certain parts of the journey, the daughter determinedly read aloud a 3 words x 4 lines passage on balloons. She was stumped by 1-2 words but when I told her how to read them, she huffed and puffed, saying that she wanted to read everything “by my own self”. (Work in progress. Trying to get her to say “by myself” in the name of grammatical English.) Such complicated are female creatures, even the youngest ones. Anyway, the moral of this story is that she kept reading the 12 words again and again until she became relatively fluent at reading the entire passage. Her persistence left me awed and surprised in equal measure. When do children lose their innate sense to try their hardest at something? Or have I been lucky that the daughter was born tenacious?

items.title: The Billionaire Bankrolling of New, Physical Print Magazines
items.text:
Over five years ago, I wrote a piece called "[An Age of Patronage](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/an-age-of-patronage/)" where I speculated how arts and research will/may work in a free world.

Basically sketching out the "value-for-value" revolution before that was cute or Lightning worked well enough for it.

## This month, I saw THREE print magazines launching/returning

**FIRST:** @asanoha and Bitcoin Art Magazine /Edition One https://stacker.news/items/1604664
This one isn't *quite* like the others -- for instance, I doubt there's a billionaire bankrolling it? -- but it's still a bet on a return to slow-form PHYSICAL MAGAZINES.

Definitely in the age of quick-hit/fast and hot takes AI slop, there's some.
Scarcity works like that, too: facing infinite generation, only the physical and human become scarce (https://stacker.news/items/1603955, https://stacker.news/items/1608788, https://stacker.news/items/1604664)

**SECOND:** LIFE magazine, a mainstay of 20th-century America, [is back](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/28/business/media/life-magazine-karlie-kloss.html). From that NYT article:

> The iconic magazine, known for its red-box logo and devotion to visual storytelling, will start publishing again next month as a quarterly print magazine.

*This*:

> It enters a fractured media landscape that is worlds away from the publication’s midcentury heights of acclaim, before the internet, social media and artificial intelligence upended the business model of magazine publishing.
> Daniel Okrent, who was the editor of Life magazine from 1992 to 1996, said that despite the value of the Life logo and the quality of the content, it was “a constantly unprofitable magazine” throughout history.

Also: run as a passion project/vanity thing for [small-time millionaire](https://www.celebritynetworth.com/richest-celebrities/models/karlie-kloss-net-worth/) and supermodel Karlie Kloss. Ruins Den's billionaire trend? No: husband is a [multibillionaire](https://www.eonline.com/news/1434962/inside-billionaire-josh-kushner-karlie-kloss-private-world). Funzies.

Also, importantly: NOT littered with ads. (Makes sense, since ad revenue isn't bankrolling them ANYWAY)

> The issue will come out on Nov. 23 as a large-format, 250-page print magazine retailing for $45, combining news photography with long-form journalism. There are no traditional print ads; instead the first issue is sponsored by Rivian and Figma.

says Wikipedia for why it closed its doors 25 years ago:

![](https://m.stacker.news/165194)

***

**THIRD:** Works in Progress.

Been seeing this a lot in my feed in recent weeks. (I imagine the algos heavily favor something you've visited/searched for recently) https://stacker.news/items/1591235, https://stacker.news/items/1598977, https://stacker.news/items/1601320

https://x.com/WorksInProgMag/status/2115617294005284869

No slop, *craft* in making beautiful things -- *and* important content.

The entire project is bankrolled by Stripe // Stripe Publishing and ultimate *their*owners, Patrick and John Collison et al.

***

It's *very* interesting to see this semi-/fake-capitalistic development, with art and storytelling and journalism be portrayed and worked on passionately by REAL and SERIOUS people, that looks and behaves like any other capitalist enterprise -- just *won't* be profit-oriented or ever aspire to making a profit.

## They're in it for the tech...

or rather, the humanity of it. The changing society. The craft and beauty and *deep meaning*.

I live this trend. And apparently, *sic semper salvatores*:

https://x.com/CharlesCMann/status/2118334333782012086

## All successful journalistic efforts were similarly "bankrolled by wealthy eccentrics"?

Yeah, I dunno. *But what did the rich ever do for us?!*

The recent anti-billionaire campaigns channeled their energy incorrectly. It's not that [the "rich" need to finance](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/an-age-of-patronage/) failing programs like Medicare, or fat, lazy Californians' health problems. They should just build shit, bankroll artists, be \_patrons\_ to us creative peeps... and churches and architecture and all the other beautiful things in human/western civ. 

## "patronage is “the tribute which opulence owes to genius.” --Edmund Burke

> If you were wealthy, **it was your moral obligation to give back to the community** – not merely by improving the lot of the poor or renovating your local church but also by supporting artists and intellectuals.

Interesting future ahead of us. Huuuuge if true.

items.title: This is my last Christmas as Santa Claus.
items.text:
Yes, it hurts just as much as I imagined it would. My daughter has reached the age where the magic comes to an end more and more questions, fewer friends who still believe in magic, and more friends confirming that it’s actually the parents who place the gifts under the tree every December 25th.

Playing the role of Santa this Christmas season was spectacular; the excitement, the happiness, the smile, and the look in my daughter’s eyes every December 25th are truly priceless. Buying gifts on the sly and stashing them away in secret, strategic spots is so much fun. I’m open to new traditions, though I’m also a bit scared and nervous about the next stages of her childhood.

I have previously made posts in which I’ve been chronicling this journey into the world of fantasy

[I managed to find the right answer to my daughter's questions about Santa Claus](https://stacker.news/items/1253270/r/bief57)

[Does Santa Claus commit labor exploitation?Questions from my 8 year old daughter](https://stacker.news/items/996626/r/bief57)

[Does the tooth fairy print money? Questions my 8-year-old daughter asks me.](https://stacker.news/items/990421/r/bief57)

About two months ago, I was walking down the street with my daughter when, out of the blue, she asked me: "Do parents pay Santa Claus to bring the gifts?"

I stayed silent, pretending I hadn’t heard, while I thought about how to respond. I considered making up a lie—an interesting story, something to keep his belief in magic alive—but then I remembered he’s nine years old; by this age, most children in the middle years of primary school no longer believe in fairy tales. I also thought about the risk of bullying, and the fact that living in a fictional world isn’t exactly healthy when reality can be so cruel. So, I simply replied, "Yes, parents have to pay." My intention was to spark some doubt and critical thinking—to plant the seed of reality without being too blunt. He immediately burst into tears, and we had to sit down on the sidewalk. I shed a few tears myself and asked him what was making him sad. He began asking questions: "How much money do they get?" "So, you’re the ones who choose the gifts?" "Back before bank transfers existed, did they pay with checks?" I cracked a joke—"Does that mean Santa Claus is basically a toy delivery service?"—and we both managed a little laugh.

I wonder if I’ve lied to him about other things, and if he suspects that the same is true when it comes to the Tooth Fairy.

We had a pleasant conversation—at least it was for me, and I hope it was for her, too. She told me that what saddened her most was that reality isn’t as fun as the idea of a magical man arriving in December on a flying sleigh to hand out toys. She also used the phrase "everything is a business" when I confirmed that, yes, we actually give money to Santa.

I wondered why we parents create these magical stories, and I told her that it’s a tradition meant to encourage the imagination. I shared that when I was a child, I enjoyed it myself; eventually, I figured out the truth, but I still helped preserve the innocence of my younger sisters while they were still little. I wanted to do the same for her, because love is the closest thing there is to magic. I explained that this is why not everyone follows this tradition—in fact, some religions even forbid it. I also explained that every person or culture constructs its own fantasy world; these can be rooted in doing good, or conversely, in causing harm—for instance, through practices like Santería or witchcraft (which are quite common here in Venezuela).

I’m left with a bitter taste of disappointment and sadness, but it was time; he still believes there’s a fellow named Saint Nicholas who delivers toys at the request of parents—maybe next year he’ll get to know "Saint Amazon" (just a joke).



Christmas 2025

1. It brought something new about Bitcoin. Can't remember last time this happened
2. I spent a lot of resources on the cinematography, and I knew it will make it stand out

![](https://m.stacker.news/165143)

items.title: EXTROPY — the 1988–1996 archive
items.text:
Extropy - "the vaccine for future shock" was a precursor to the Cypherpunk Mailing List and home to many of the ideas that went on to be discussed by that community.

This (AI generated website) has digitized the contents of a great number of their issues. There are some great articles in here including an article on [exercise and longevity by Fran Finney](https://extropy.agoraops.org/issues/09/exercise-and-longevity/), an article about [digital cash and privacy by Hal Finney](https://extropy.agoraops.org/issues/10/protecting-privacy-with-electronic-cash/), and something about [Creole Physics and the Credit Theory of Identity](https://extropy.agoraops.org/issues/10/mark-miller-interview-pt1/) by Dave Krieger, among many others.

You could do worse than to spend some time reading these.

items.title: The Insatiable Demand for Alpha (Net Interest, Marc Rubinstein)
items.text:
What to do about natural-dividend windfalls is a theme on Den's mind this year https://stacker.news/items/1589657 https://stacker.news/items/1565551 https://stacker.news/items/1515430

![](https://m.stacker.news/165141)

> Today, the Alaska Permanent Fund has assets of $88 billion. It’s not as big as Norway’s oil fund, which we [discussed](https://www.netinterest.co/p/the-biggest-investor-in-the-world) some time ago, but it’s the closest America has to a sovereign wealth fund. Each year, the state is allowed to draw 5% from the fund to finance government services and to pay a dividend to residents. This year, eligible residents will each receive a check for $1,200.

But interestingly, at first it consisted *only* of bonds -- even though this was, in principle, a perpetual fund lasting looong into the future https://stacker.news/items/1609745

> . In 1999, its mandate was broadened to allow a 5% allocation to alternative investments and, in 2004, the fund made its first foray into hedge funds. \[Those] were made through a fund-of-funds program. Alaska hired three managers to select hedge funds on its behalf but performance was disappointing. In the ten years through to 2016, those hedge funds generated a 3.4% annualized return

How about this for epic alpha investing? Nine years, 6.7% annualized return *and no down years*. Sexy:

> The shift in approach paid off. Alaska now allocates to 18 managers, accounting for 8% of its total portfolio. When markets slid in 2022, the hedge fund part of its portfolio was up about 8%. In the nine years since the restructuring, the average annualized return of the hedge fund portfolio has been 6.7% with no down years and a low correlation to overall markets.

![](https://m.stacker.news/165147)

## "The problem, though, is that “the more money we push into absolute return, the harder it is to get that really special return because the good funds are capacity constrained.”

**I'm sure that's why Undisc can't rule the ROI league at** @Team_Predyx **anymore!**

THANKFULLY,

> Perhaps Millennium has an answer to that.
> When Alaska first invested, Millennium was a $35 billion fund; it is now knocking on the door of $100 billion. Its return in October was [weak](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-03/major-hedge-funds-mostly-lose-in-nowhere-to-hide-october?srnd=undefined), down 2.3%, but that sits within its risk tolerance limits and compared with other funds, it could have been worse. How it performs in November, when many funds have struggled, will be key.

...but, "to see what Millennium is up to," we need to bypass a paywall. And Den is cheap (poor? lazy?!) so there's no Net Interest subscription!

We shall never find out what the secret Millennium hedge fund sauce is.

items.title: A Lodging for Wayfaring Men Book Club: Chapter 3
items.text:
*Welcome to the sixth week of our book club reading* A Lodging for Wayfaring Men. *We're reading one chapter every two weeks, so we'll today be discussing Chapter 3 (but in between-weeks we are having a look at the essays in Appendix A. They are short and accessible).*

*You can find the book club reading schedule here:* https://stacker.news/items/1582413

***

The story of people who are trying to build unstoppable, unregulated markets on the internet is really cool. Unfortunately, Rosenberg is not doing the best job of it. I often feel like he glosses over the most interesting parts and includes quite a lot of stuff that doesn't add much to the story at all.

For instance, I'm not quite sure what the purpose of the biomedical peptides "Brain Flush" storyline is. Sure, that's cool, too -- but why do the freedom market people also need to be inventing a thing that cures you from all your emotional baggage? And then there's the free love stuff.

I can see how it all kind of connects in the theme of regulation impeding humans from being as fully developed as they can be, but it's too widespread to do justice to any single storyline. I would love to see more character development or even discussion of ideas, the characters just don't need to be saving the world along quite so many verticals.

Still, Rosenberg doesn't fail to include a number of interesting points that made me stop and think. The greatest of these, at least in this chapter, was this:

> But the Internet opened up a virgin territory for us. A territory that is a hell of a lot harder to control than a geographic territory. And because the basic structure of cyberspace is distributed, not centralized, we have a built-in advantage.
>
> What we are doing is a natural progression of the digital revolution. What the governments are trying to do is to reroute the digital revolution, against its nature, to serve their desire for centralized dominion.
>
> "The Internet must be protected. We can't let it become a tool of the old territorial rulers. So, we are building a center of private interactions, where rulers cannot intrude. It was a strange moment when several of us looked around and said to each other, 'Oh my God, we can't let this opportunity pass, and we are the adults. We have to step in adn see to this; we're here, we're able, and it has fallen to us."

I really strongly believe in this vision for the internet, and since I've been reading some of the archives of the Cypherpunks Mailing List lately, it doubly resonated. It seems that using the Internet as the home of truly free markets was developed in tandem with the internet itself. At the first meeting of the Cypherpunks they played a game that simulated using the internet for exactly this purpose https://stacker.news/items/1609744/r/Scoresby.

The internet has been in full flower for many decades and bitcoin has been around for almost two, but for me at least, the question of whether such unregulated markets exist is still unclear https://stacker.news/items/1608631/r/Scoresby.

So, what do you think: has the internet fallen to regulation, surveillance and control, or is there still hope that we can play the crypto anarchy game for real?

# How is this battle for the internet going? Are we winning? Or are the scales tipping in favor of the government?

items.title: Javokhir Sindarov vs Gukesh Dommaraju: Chess Championship (FIDE, Peter Svidler)
items.text:
Short interview with Peter Svidler, a legend of the game who, himself, challenged for the title in the early 2000s. While no longer an active player (mostly just a coach or commentator these days,) at his current, inactive, rating he'd qualify as **#42** in the world.

Here he discusses the recent form of the two championship contenders *and* comments on their respective style. Actually, he says, "style" doesn't make much sense for these youngsters who came off age in the era of computers... having practiced with and analyzed games with them since forever.

> People who reach this level are pretty much *always* universal... so talking about stylistic preferences for someone playing for the world championship was KIND OF ridiculous because they could do everything.
> but *this* generation of players seem to be a lot more concrete -- and a lot less hung up on the things which were obsessions for players of previous generations: things like "sound" positional play. 
>
> It's not that they *can't* play positional chess, of course they can, but their formative years were spent working with computers and that very much changes how they view the game. Because if there's one thing that computers teach you, time and time again, it is that **a lot more is affordable; a lot more is defensible; a lot more is possible**, if you can just calculate really, really cleanly.

## "It's a lot more natural to them to play dynamic chess than to play positional chess"

**What will be the key factors in the championship game?**

Openings won't matter... everyone is extremely well prepared, and everybody plays the same openings.

Psych and mentality, keeping yourself (and your emotions) in check(!) will matter.

> 60% \[Javokhir] is already very high; even with the kind of year that Gukesh has had, going higher than 55-45 isn't justifiable. Gukesh is still a very strong player, it's still a very specific format. **I'm sort of willing to go 55-45 Sindarov** but I don't think I'm willing to go higher.

Also, checking in on the Predyx odds:

![](https://m.stacker.news/165195)

## *amagad, prediction markets are efficient!!*

...the polymarket people are *too* aggressively in favor of Javokhir ([75-25](https://polymarket.com/event/2026-world-chess-championship-winner))

items.title: Blok's Stock Review: Portland General Electric Company (POR)
items.text:
***USD/BTC = $75,814***
 ***Block 974,944***

## Today's Stock: Portland General Electric Company (POR)

![](https://m.stacker.news/165155)

Portland General Electric is a regulated electric utility serving Portland and the northern Willamette Valley in Oregon. It generates, buys, transmits and distributes power to homes and businesses. 

## My Thoughts 💭

One share costs 60,609 sats ($45.95). It pays $2.205 a year in dividends, 2,908 sats a share, so it would take about 21 years of dividends to break even on one share at that price. The P/E is 20.0, a 20 year payback on earnings. There is no payback at all on free cash flow because free cash flow is negative. Let's review the fundamentals to determine if this stock is worth spending sats on.

## PE:

![](https://m.stacker.news/165157)

P/E 20.0 TTM on earnings of $273M. Simply Wall St calls it good value against the peer average of 22.2 and against its fair P/E of 20.8, but expensive against the electric utilities industry average of 19.5. The price sits right on my rule 3 line of under 20, not below it.

## Expected Growth:

![](https://m.stacker.news/165159)

Earnings are forecast to grow 14.35 percent a year and revenue 7.4 percent a year. EPS is expected to grow 39 percent over the next 3 years against 19 percent for the industry. Forecast ROE rises to 9.3 percent from 6.3 percent today. Add the 4.8 percent dividend yield to the growth and the projected total return is about 19 percent a year. That clears my 15 percent Bitcoin bear hurdle but not the 30 percent bull hurdle.

## Revenues and expenses:


![](https://m.stacker.news/165160)


Revenue $3.55B TTM with net income of $273M, a 7.68 percent net margin. Cash from operations is $959M a year, but free cash flow is negative $416M a year and Simply Wall St calls the trend alarming. Rule 5 fails. A utility pouring cash into the grid still has to show positive free cash flow sooner or later.

## Balance Sheet:

![](https://m.stacker.news/165161)

Total debt $5.43B against cash and short term investments of just $69M. Debt to equity is 125.4 percent and interest is covered only 2.1 times by earnings. Normal leverage for a utility, but rules 1 and 4 fail outright on my sheet.

## Dividend:

![](https://m.stacker.news/165162)

Yield 4.8 percent on $2.205 a share a year, which passes rule 2 with room. The payout ratio is 90 percent of earnings though, so rule 6 fails, and Simply Wall St says the dividend is not well covered by earnings or free cash flows. The next payment is $0.55 a share, ex date December 22, 2026, pay date January 15, 2027. Share count is also rising, a buyback yield of negative 6.5 percent, which dilutes the holder while the dividend goes out the door.

## Bitcoin per share:

None. POR holds no BTC on its balance sheet.

## Ownership breakdown:


![](https://m.stacker.news/165163)


Institutions hold 99.5 percent, insiders 0.435 percent. The top 25 shareholders own about 71 percent, with BlackRock the largest at 15.7 percent.

## Leadership:

![](https://m.stacker.news/165164)

CEO Maria Pope has run the company since October 2017. Her total compensation is $7.58M, below the $8.42M average for companies of similar size, and Simply Wall St flags no excessive pay concern. Rule 7 passes.

## Blok's 9 rules: 3 of 9

1. ❌ Debt $5.43B with a debt to equity ratio of 125.4 percent
2. ✅ Dividend yield 4.8 percent
3. ⚠️ P/E 20.0 sits right on the line, not under 20
4. ❌ Cash $69M against debt of $5.43B
5. ❌ Free cash flow is negative $416M
6. ❌ Payout ratio 90 percent
7. ✅ CEO pay $7.58M is below the similar size average of $8.42M
8. ✅ Energy, a regulated electric utility
9. ⚠️ Projected return near 19 percent clears the 15 percent bear hurdle only

## Lyn's Lens:

The first pillar passes at the door. POR is a profitable company with hard regulated assets and real earnings. Her entry math for mid teens growth plus a near 5 percent yield supports roughly 25x to 30x earnings, and on trailing EPS of $2.29 that implies about $57 to $69. The $45.95 price works on earnings with room to spare. Cash is where her lens turns. Free cash flow is negative, the dividend is not covered by it, and the balance sheet carries real leverage. Lyn's Lens says the price works on earnings, not on cash flow.

## Closing take

While I am a fan of investing in utilities I think buying and holding 60k worth of sats should perform better than this utility company. The high leverage and low FCF makes me think this is a dead but essential company. Investors won’t get rich holding this but it will take a long grind to get the initial investment back while inflation will continue to erode the value of the dollar. This is a pass for me!

Price context: $45.95 sits near the low end of its range between $43.26 and $54.62 over the past year, down about 4 percent in that year. Simply Wall St puts its cash flow value at $46.60 and the analyst consensus target at $52.27.

items.title: OpenBitcoin.com: A new bitcoin block explorer with guides tools and games
items.text:
I have been building a bitcoin block explorer and I feel it's good enough to show:

[https://openbitcoin.com](https://openbitcoin.com)

The site runs its own hardware, bitcoin node and address index. No third-party blockchain API used.

Inside the site:

- Explorer: blocks, transactions and addresses at root-level URLs. (very important, a feature I always wanted with other explorers, a quick easy way to query an address) For example you can type openbitcoin.com/block_number_here or openbitcoin.com/txid_here or openbitcoin.com/address_here to load the page instantly without visiting the site to use the search bar :)

- Node census (openbitcoin.com/nodes): reachable nodes counted by my own P2P crawler, 8,958 nodes from 92 countries last run.

- Rich list (openbitcoin.com/rich-list): top 10,000 addresses and balance distributions.

- Prices: spot price as a median of three exchanges, with a quick conversion tool on the front page.

- Tools: fee calculator, address validator, message verifier, QR generator, and key tools built to be downloaded and run offline.

- Guides: on confirmations, UTXOs, self-custody, stuck transactions and more. Newbie friendly.

- Games (openbitcoin.com/games): three arcade games built on real bitcoin mechanics, stack blocks, clear a mempool backlog, and a slot machine that plays the actual odds of guessing a private key.

The website is open source. What stays private is my server's operational layer.

Would appreciate any feedback, happy to contribute to the community.

items.title: Chess-November Continues: Introducing the Total Chess Championship
items.text:
Yes, I'm back making *another* chess market. And *yes*, there's *another* major chess tournament this month.

## The chess world is insane: drama everywhere.

Meaning, importantly, that Javokhir and Gukesh are *not* participating. (duh) https://stacker.news/items/1610211

This format is sort of more along the lines of what Magnus wanted FIDE to turn toward, with a mix of time controls and an open tournament sort of situation rather than the grueling one-on-one matches the world championship consists of https://stacker.news/items/1608324

So, our beloved chess No. 1 and GOAT is here, pwning it off.

![](https://m.stacker.news/165197)

![](https://m.stacker.news/165198)

![](https://m.stacker.news/165199)

I kind of *don't* quite understand all the nuances of the format (but as you follow along the tourney, it usually makes more sense!!) https://stacker.news/items/1609473

...and if it doesn't, I shall be around to help! (or, you know, just ask your favorite AI; what do I care -.-)

***

ANYWAY:

There's **24** players in the tournament, about half with roughly *0%* chance of winning. I couldn't be arsed funding/specifying *all* potential winners, so I just included the tops/my favs -- and shoved all the others into, well, "Others."

Since we're all degenerate gamblers here, I thoroughly expect "Team Hans" (https://stacker.news/items/1609473?commentId=1609678) to bid up his poor chances (currently at 7%) to higher than that. I launched it with these probabilities (and then added some neat bids myself so the market doesn't look so sad!)

- **Magnus**: 30%
- **Nodirbek**: 20%
- **Pragg**: 10%
- **Niemann**: 5%
- **Others** (including Rapport, Arjun, Fabiano, Nepo, Anish, Shak) = 35%

Magnus is \_obviously\_ the top favorite in every tournament he plays, but what's so cool about elite chess in the ano 2026 is that *on a good day* any of these guys can beat him in a single game or two... *especially* in the shorter time controls where the youngsters (Nodirbek, Alireza, Niemann etc) definitely have a good chance.

![](https://m.stacker.news/165201)

## Go forth and bet, my chessy friends

**And let's look forward to a wonderful month of even-more wonderful chess!**

items.title: There's 0.2024 BTC hidden inside Pierre Noizat's book (French edition)
items.text:
## [L'énergie, face cachée de la monnaie](https://www.kobo.com/us/en/ebook/l-energie-face-cachee-de-la-monnaie)

Nobody has cracked it in 2 years, but recently, we started to receive a lot of emails asking for clues.
Initially, 7 clues were released, but even with frontier AI tools, the wallet still hasn't been drained.

recap and more clues below👇

![](https://m.stacker.news/165108)

***

First clue: “A picture is worth a thousand words, but eight pictures are worth fourteen.”

2. Then there are 2 Olympic years.
3. Department of origin.
4. 2 in the table of contents.
5. 2 in a chapter that deals with a central theme of the book.
6. Une traduction en anglais est en cours.
7. In the end, decentralized networks always prevail.

This isn't a clue but a clarification that could be useful: how does one go from a 24-word mnemonic passphrase to a Bitcoin address?

More specifically, how does one find the private key of an address from a mnemonic phrase?

***

Seven clues were revealed between August 15 and September 26, 2024.
As of now, that has not been enough, despite the shrewdness of the bitcoiners.

There will therefore be 7 additional clues (numbered 8 to 14): one every Thursday until December 19 inclusive, then 3 clues on

All the words are found on the normalized list [http://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039/](http://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0039/).

The first 21 words to find (in the book) are in French and the last 3 in English. Then replace each of the 21 French words with the one of the same rank in the english.txt list

To verify that you have correctly found the first 23 words, the word staff (1697) can be used in the 24th position to form a valid mnemonic phrase compatible with wallets that allow the use of 24-word phrases, including Blockstream's wallet.

In fact, any of these 8 words can be used in the 24th position as the checksum word:
alien
detect
flip
gas
organ
peasant
staff
trigger

All you need to do then is replace it with the 24th word (which is NOT one of the 8 words above) and calculate the “seed”.

The first 14 words are contained in the book's images, taken in order. The words million, minutes, and opinions are not part of the solution because they are used multiple times in the images or in the plural.
The 13th and 14th words are on the cover.

The Olympic years are linked to the author's biography (15th and 16th words). Be careful, there is false information on certain unreliable sites.
The 17th word is linked to the author's name.

The 18th and 19th words are in the summary.

The words in the 22nd, 23rd, and 24th positions form a slogan used in 2024 by a brand known worldwide, inspired by a title from the group Tomorrow x Together.

***

Get the book here:
[https://konsensus.net/books/?b=lenergie-face-cachee-de-la-monnaie-2](https://konsensus.net/books/?b=lenergie-face-cachee-de-la-monnaie-2)
(also available in English)

Curious to see who's going to crack it

`Burns and McDonnell has completed Missouris largest membrane bioreactor system as part of the city of Republics $145 million wastewater infrastructure program, about 1,916 BTC at todays rate ($145,000,000 / $75,673).`

The upgraded Republic Water Reclamation Facility now treats 5 million gallons per day. The expansion is a first of its kind treatment solution in Missouri and helps the city handle compliance challenges and prepare for future growth.

The $145 million program also includes peak wet weather improvements and three collection system projects.` The city financed it through direct allocations, state revolving fund loans and revenue bonds. `Republic has been working with Burns and McDonnell on a water and wastewater master plan since 2017.

The project used progressive design build, a first for Republic. When early estimates came in over budget, the team used value engineering to bring the price down while keeping the original treatment goals.

"Working as one team helped us respond to cost pressures, plan construction around ongoing operations and prepare staff to operate the new systems," said Alli White, operations manager at Burns and McDonnell.

`The water market stays hot. Burns and McDonnell is bullish on water going into 2027, and McCarthy Building Cos. president of water Jaren Murphy told Construction Dive that almost every large municipality now has a billion dollar plus capital improvement plan in motion.`

I think the water market will continue to be hot!

items.title: Why Milei's Chainsaw Revolution Required Restraint
items.text:
> **Critics are divided as Javier Milei takes gradual, constrained steps toward the radical free market he campaigned on.**
>
> In December 2023, as the sound of a chainsaw echoed through Buenos Aires, Javier Milei swept into the Casa Rosada, and pro-market Austrian School economists cheered his victory. Nearly three years later, many libertarians are disappointed. They keep asking themselves: Did they vote for [Rothbard](https://mises.org/profile/murray-n-rothbard), only to get another central planner?
>
> He campaigned on a platform that was not merely reformist but explicitly abolitionist. He promised to end the Central Bank, dollarize the economy, and rein in the interventionist state. The Central Bank of Argentina (BCRA) still opens its doors every morning. The government did not [lift restrictions](https://www.elibrary.imf.org/view/journals/002/2025/219/article-A001-en.xml) on moving foreign currencies until April 2025. To an orthodox libertarian, all of this might still look like central planning.
>
> That criticism has divided free-market thinkers, including Austrian economists. Hans-Hermann Hoppe, for example, has criticized Milei for not acting radically enough. [Milei responded sharply in an interview](https://x.com/LibertarianDuty/status/1867202040742522933) and accused Hoppe of lacking sufficient knowledge of monetary economics. Milei argued that the demands for immediate change ignore important risks, such as hyperinflation.
>
> Milei believes that poorly timed good policy can lead to the worst outcome. He believes that the path to a free market must begin with ending persistent budget deficits, not lifting capital controls. He hopes this approach will advance his political agenda while limiting political tensions and inflation risk.
>
> Milei’s background as a macroeconomist explains his thinking. In this sense, his approach is technocratic because he prioritizes the economic conditions needed to achieve his free-market goals, even if that requires more nuance than his ideological promises.
>
> [**...read more at thedailyeconomy.org**](https://thedailyeconomy.org/article/why-mileis-chainsaw-revolution-required-restraint/)

items.title: In Search of Freedom: Life, Death, and Sovereignty in the Himalaya
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/164458)

*I’m sitting in a dusty hotel room in Kathmandu, attempting to call a Spanish airline about my missing luggage.*
*“We’ll have to email our ground staff contractor,” they say.*
*I try to protest. “My trek starts tomorrow!”*
*“Please check your email later today, sir.”*
*I listen to the click of the agent hanging up the phone.*

The hotel is nestled precisely in the middle of Thamel, the tourist district with its colourful flags, rooftop gardens, and too-narrow streets. There is plenty to do in the capital, but after three days of chasing my lost bag in a Kafkaesque system of virtual shrugs and missed callbacks, my energy wanes. I am trapped in the antipresent, unable to visit any tourist attractions, only capable of reconnecting to the hotel WiFi to refresh my emails for the 800th time in the hope of news. With nothing but time, I feel utterly trapped.

During a 2018 volunteering trip to Nepal, I waited for my opportunity to walk the Annapurna Circuit: a two-week hiking route crossing high paths and winding through tiny Buddhist villages. Instead, I got a call to fly back to the UK. My father had been diagnosed with bowel cancer, and it was terminal. He was the one who introduced me to hiking, taught me to be patient when faced with another false peak, to understand the swirling patterns of clouds, to clean my kit, to be prepared for sudden change, to appreciate in the silence of the wilderness, to be present. Near the end, we talked a lot about hiking.

“When you see a mountain,” he said, “think of me.”
I can’t remember what I said in return.

It took eight years to get back to Nepal — grief, travel, COVID, relocation, work, money, rule changes, and procrastination saw to that. After all my posturing about being an advocate for freedom, living my life exactly how I wanted, my fear of closure held me back. I wouldn’t gain perspective until I’d seen those mountains again.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164459)

*Finally, after another two-day delay, I take the first steps of my 18-day trek. The Manang Valley bathes in bright sunlight. We pass apple orchards and fields of buckwheat as we climb to Lower Pisang, but after nearly a week stuck in the hotel, I feel like I could run up the path for hours. I’m not doing this alone; there are ten in my group — other travellers looking for answers in the hills. We get to know each other in the brief moments when we’re not gasping for breath in the thinning air.*

That night, I fire up my Kindle and read [*The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas*](https://shsdavisapes.pbworks.com/f/Omelas.pdf). It’s one of my all-time favourites, a short story that’s more of a thought experiment. Ursula Le Guin presents a Utopian society of harmony, peace, and joy. In Omelas, life is wonderful for every resident except one: a miserable child, suffering alone in a dungeon. Most residents can ignore the one person whose incarceration guarantees their joy and freedom, but the few who can’t leave the citadel forever.

Maybe it’s hubris, but I’ve always considered myself one of those who ‘walk away’. I’ve been willing to give up convenience to claw back some of the sovereignty I’d lost through a corporate job and living in a mediocre London suburb. And here I was on a legendary remote hiking route, perhaps not scaling peaks, but at least challenging myself, climbing higher than I’ve ever been.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164462)

*The nights are cold at 4000m above sea level, and my wardrobe is more suited to the Spanish summer than sub-zero temperatures. As we hike farther up, across metal suspension bridges and past well-insulated herds of yaks, I wear my father’s old gear — a down vest and the bright red* *waterproof. It’s not a homage; it’s purely practical. Still, it gives me some kind of connection.*

I feel him silently judging me for walking the ‘tourist trail’. He always had to plan the route and bring every bit of kit himself, while a Nepalese porter carries my luggage strapped directly to their forehead. He would also have loved seeing the world’s highest peaks up close and listening to the guides' explanations of the dangers, the routes, the climbers. We all live the battle of comfort vs sovereignty.

The ‘tea house’ hotels in the Manang valley have a few more mod cons than expected. Some even have hot showers. But today, the power for the whole village is out. As the sun sets, my roommate and I read by the light of our headtorches.

Before the trip, I’d just finished reading *The Gulag Archipelago*, Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn’s brutal account of the anti-freedoms of Communist Russia. That night, I search for a quote that jumped off the page when I read it: ‘All those years in our cells and our huts, the state’s electricity had seared our souls, and now, darkness was bliss.’ Sometimes, our only freedom comes through stoic minimalism and absence. I turned off my reading light and listened to the darkness.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164463)

*I’m in bed with a worsening cold. The lack of doctors and pharmacies doesn’t seem so quaint when you are coughing up your lungs. The 5,416m Thorong La Pass plays on my mind, and I struggle to sleep. It’s not just me; another member of the group has a virus, and most of the others are blowing their runny noses in the dry mountain air. We take each day slowly, climbing 500m in altitude, and putting one foot in front of the other. There aren’t any other options: turning back involves walking too, and I don’t like going backwards.*

By this point, we’ve walked 80km or so. [Karl Bushby](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8rz38jr50go) has just finished walking 50,000km after circumnavigating the globe by foot. I watched a video on his trip just before setting off on mine, and I was most impressed by the fact he had no desire to break records, no charity campaign, no press team. “Every fibre of my being,” he says, “every day, has been what I'm doing right now.”

Along the way, between icy paths and sneezes, I hit upon the idea that walking is trustless. That’s why it is so freeing to Karl Bushby and to all of us. You don’t rely on anyone or anything else. It is the rhythm of taking one step at a time. Sometimes things go as expected; sometimes they don't. But freedom is not about control. It depends on adapting to your surroundings and being in sync with the path. Each day, the tea houses serve another group of foreigners. Monks in the small temples perform another ceremony, another meditation. The kitchens produce another hundred plates of dal bhat, accompanied by ginger tea for the sniffling guests. The sun rises over snowy peaks again.

One of the guys in our group walked to Everest Base Camp more than 20 years ago. Things were quite primitive back then. He told me the soundtrack of those two weeks was the constant *thunk* of cattle bells. That was his rhythm, his surroundings. He bought a heavy metal bell in a Kathmandu market at the end of his trip and still displays it proudly in his New Jersey house.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164464)

*It’s 4 am and -15℃ on the day we climb over the pass and down the other side. Lines of headtorches light the steep path up, and the snow crunches under boots fitted with temporary metal spikes. The path ahead is backed up because a girl from another group has fainted. Her partner attempts to carry her up on piggyback, but stops after just a few steps.*

*As we wait for the last members of our party to arrive, we hop from foot to foot to keep warm. Frank, a German realtor who lives in Cape Town, excitedly tells us he has the WiFi password for a teahouse we’ve just passed. ‘Who cares?’ I think. ‘You’ve flown all the way here to cross this pass, and you’ve gotten up in the dark to do it. Why do you need WiFi?’*

Later, after the girl who collapsed has passed us riding on a yak, after we’ve taken our photos at the top, and after we’ve descended to 3,800 meters and bathed in the sun of the afternoon, I reflect on Frank and his need for WiFi passwords. Yes, we are all plugged into our digital worlds, but if you can’t spend a few hours away from it, are you really free at all?

I think about the amount of time I spent that day completely disconnected, staring at the contrast of birds of prey crossing white peaks and soaring up into a blue sky. Why do we struggle to think beyond the next unit of time? The next breath, photo, coffee break, the next day, the next WiFi access point. Why do we need to extract immediate value from our physical world?

I can’t always rein in my differences from the group. Not everyone has waited eight long years to reconnect with their father by climbing a Nepalese mountain. This is every fibre of my being, not just a social media photo op. My father would have loved to build a homestead, to fix machines, grow cattle, and walk the land, but he chose a secure life so his children could do that.

The next days we pass through small towns celebrating *Dashain* — a time for families, giving thanks, and taking stock. We stay with a local family and experience life in a small town; while we eat set meals and walk to a strict schedule, it feels like all the Nepalis around us are making their own choices.

We watch old ladies harvesting millet and corn. Heavy machinery continues to shift the earth of roads and riverbanks affected by landslides. We see new entrepreneurs opening restaurants, tea houses, and local stores. I speak to Ram, one of our guides, who is working through the festival period to put his kids through college in Japan. Everyone must hustle to improve their lot because saving in Rupees is futile. Even with remittances from those working abroad, Nepal is constantly playing catch-up. Everyone is building a better life here; no one expects it to be easy.

***

![](https://m.stacker.news/164466)

*My final day is spent in Kathmandu. A few of us travel to Durbar Square to see the world’s only living goddess. The Kumari is a young girl selected from a northern village. There are strict physical and mental tests as well as a birthdate that matches specific astrological criteria. She is taken from her parents to live in an opulent palace, where her feet may never touch the ground below. If she sheds a drop of blood, she is cast out into the realm of the mortals and is replaced by a new Kumari. Hindus and Buddhists alike come to see her, hoping to be blessed by one of her three daily appearances at her palace window. The current Kumari is just three years old. After waiting an hour for her to appear, I feel like her nervous little wave is an anticlimax. The crowd still gasps.*

Later, it hits me that she is the living embodiment of the child in *The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas*. Instead of being tortured or in pain, she is doted on. She has expensive gowns, extravagant makeup, a team of handlers, tutors, and adoring fans, but she is cursed. Her childhood is stolen, and she is imprisoned to bring others luck, joy, and religious harmony. She cannot play, shout, hide, misbehave, cry, laugh, or neglect her duties. She cannot walk where she pleases. To tourists, the Kumari is a sweet anomaly, a curious tradition. To Nepalis, she is a living goddess. Almost everyone is happy with this arrangement.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164460)

I went to Nepal to reconnect with emotions I had long since buried. Curiously, I saw glimpses of freedom instead of apparitions of my father. Sometimes I saw them in the hawks cruising high above, sometimes in the industrious lives of locals, and sometimes in the restrictions of those trapped in digital worlds or religious constructs.

If there is one thing I learned on this journey across the Annapurna mountains, it is that freedom is gained one step at a time. You have to know which direction you are heading, and you must understand what you are leaving behind.

items.title: Claude Code's “Don't Ask Again” File Exposes 1122 Passwords and Keys
items.text:
Passwords and API keys that developers typed into commands they approved in Claude Code are sitting in public GitHub repositories, where anyone can read them.

When a user selects "Yes, and don't ask again," Anthropic's AI coding assistant can save the command, word-for-word, including the secret, in a project settings file.

items.title: My daughter’s tenacious spirit
items.text: Travelled to the end of the world (aka Pasir Ris), but I wasn’t deterred by the long commuting time. See, I went prepared because I had brought along the Berries textbook. On certain parts of the journey, the daughter determinedly read aloud a 3 words x 4 lines passage on balloons. She was stumped by 1-2 words but when I told her how to read them, she huffed and puffed, saying that she wanted to read everything “by my own self”. (Work in progress. Trying to get her to say “by myself” in the name of grammatical English.) Such complicated are female creatures, even the youngest ones. Anyway, the moral of this story is that she kept reading the 12 words again and again until she became relatively fluent at reading the entire passage. Her persistence left me awed and surprised in equal measure. When do children lose their innate sense to try their hardest at something? Or have I been lucky that the daughter was born tenacious?
